fullText:
It's common sense that common cents are getting less use in Americans' daily lives. Congress already took action to eliminate the lowest rung — the penny — and now another coin collecting dust in people's wallets could be on the chopping block next.

The House and Senate both passed bills earlier this year aimed at eliminating the penny once and for all. The bipartisan Common Cents Act was unanimously approved in each chamber, but has yet to get President Donald Trump's signature to become law.

It followed the Treasury Department announcing last December that the U.S. Mint would no longer produce pennies, which at the time cost more than three times their value to make.

TRUMP’S FIRST-YEAR GOVERNMENT OVERHAUL DELIVERS CHANGE WASHINGTON HASN’T SEEN SINCE THE 1960S

Now, lawmakers want the administration to act on another portion of their bill, which would direct the Treasury to study the potential of making the nickel with cheaper materials than are currently used.

"If it costs 13 cents to make a five-cent coin, Washington should fix the problem instead of wasting more taxpayer money," House GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain, R-Mich., told Fox News Digital. "My bill gives Treasury a path to make nickels at a lower cost without disrupting how Americans use them. It is a simple reform that saves money and brings a little more common sense to government.

Sen. Cynthia Lummis, R-Wyo., who led the bill in the Senate, told Fox News Digital, "More and more Americans are paying with credit cards, debit cards, and stablecoins for everyday purchases that once would have been made with cash or coins."

"The half-cent coin was retired when it was no longer needed, and the penny has now reached that same point. It’s my hope that we can find a cheaper way to produce the nickel so that it remains economically viable for years to come," Lummis said.

Nickels are produced at a loss to taxpayers of roughly eight cents per coin, according to the latest data. They are currently made of a mixture comprised of 25% nickel and 75% copper.

The Common Cents Act "authorizes a lower-cost nickel composition if testing shows it will reduce production costs without significantly disrupting coin-operated machines," such as vending machines, according to a release on McClain's site.

But it's not clear that there is much appetite for ending nickel production altogether, at least not yet.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News in May 2025 that he believed the U.S. could "retool" the nickel to make it cheaper to produce.

In its December 2025 announcement, the Trump administration projected immediate cost savings of $56 million in stopping penny minting.

But the decision could be reversed by any future administration unless Trump signs the bill into law. The White House did not respond to a request for comment on whether and when the president plans to do so.

title: GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers breaks with Trump and calls to end Canada tariffs
description:
WASHINGTON — Republican U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers appears to be breaking with President Donald Trump on another key issue less than a month before Election Day.
"Drinking a Labatt and watching the Red Wings, man, it just doesn't get any more Michigan than that," Rogers said in a new ad released Oct. 7.
fullText:
WASHINGTON — Republican U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers appears to be breaking with President Donald Trump on another key issue less than a month before Election Day.

"Drinking a Labatt and watching the Red Wings, man, it just doesn't get any more Michigan than that," Rogers said in a new ad released Oct. 7. "Here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war now."

The statement marks the second time in recent weeks that Rogers spoke out — without criticizing Trump by name — against one of the president's unpopular initiatives. This time, Rogers is calling for an end to Trump's widespread trade war against Canada, America's second-biggest trading partner, while drinking a Canadian beer that's banned from import under the president's latest trade restrictions.

The Republican Senate nominee also split with Trump on the Iran war in late September, saying it "needs to end and end quickly."

Rogers' public shift on tariffs comes amid mounting opposition in Michigan to Trump's tariffs and GOP concerns that voters will reject their candidates up and down the ballot for failing to address cost-of-living concerns. Election Day is Nov. 3, though more than 200,000 Michiganians have already cast absentee ballots.

Trump in recent weeks has derisively called Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney "governor," labeled Canadian officials "nasty" and has complained that Canada is "one of the worst countries in the world to deal with," among other insults.

"They want to have a deal with us. They call us all the time. The problem is that they've treated the United States very unfairly," the Republican president told reporters in late September.

Republican Senate hopeful Rogers debuted the ad the day before he is set to face off in his first debate against Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed in Grand Rapids. The 30-second spot features Rogers wearing a flannel shirt and sitting at a bar stool at Bigg's Bar & Grill on Gratiot Avenue in Chesterfield Township.

More: Most Michigan voters oppose Trump tariffs on Canada, poll shows

A year ago, Rogers accused Democrats of "fear mongering" over Trump's tariffs, and said the president's tariff policy had "put the American people back in the driver's seat."

"President Trump is right to put America First, and tariffs are necessary when countries cheat American workers. But trade isn't one-size-fits-all," Rogers posted on social media on Aug. 29.

In an interview last month, Rogers again defended some of Trump's global tariffs and argued they had helped bring some manufacturing back to the U.S., pointing to General Motors Co.'s decision to move production of the Chevy Silverado pickup truck from Mexico to its Orion Township assembly plant.

Rogers did acknowledge that the tariffs against Canada are going to pinch Michigan consumers and said his team had conversations with the Trump administration about them.

"This is why you want to send somebody back (to Washington) who can have a conversation about what's working for Michigan and what might not work for Michigan, if you send somebody back that all they want to do is get on TikTok and talk about President Trump, we're not going to fix up one single problem," Rogers told The Detroit News.

"But if you send a guy like me back, we're going to have this conversation."

Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, by contrast, has frequently bashed Trump and Rogers over the ongoing trade war with Michigan's international neighbor, calling the Canadian tariffs "chaotic" and costly.

El-Sayed on Wednesday accused Rogers of flip-flopping again.

"Must have had one too many of those LaBatts, Mike. You cheerled this tariff war from the beginning and you're flip-flopping now because your poll numbers are in free fall," El-Sayed posted on X.com in response to Rogers' ad.

"Donald is the reason we're in a trade war. And he's the reason you're running. Not a serious person."

El-Sayed at an August campaign event said that Canadians "are the only people I know who will preemptively apologize for something they never did ... You gotta be an a------ to pick a trade war with Canada. I'm so sorry, like, they're like the nicest people on Earth."

A Detroit News/WDIV-TV (Channel 4) poll conducted just before Labor Day found that less than one-third (29%) of 600 likely general election voters in Michigan approve of Trump's decision to impose 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, including cement, wine, dairy and hockey sticks.

Nearly two-thirds (64%) said they disapprove, according to the survey conducted by the Lansing-based Glengariff Group polling firm Aug. 31 to Sept. 3. The poll has a margin of error of plus or minus four percentage points.

The overwhelming majority of Democratic (93%) and independent (73%) poll participants opposed the tariffs, while most Republicans support them — though there is division within the GOP. About 1 in 4 (24%) of base GOP voters disapprove.

"There is just wholesale opposition to these tariffs," pollster Richard Czuba said of the poll results. "And what really stands out to me is Michiganders understand the financial impact of these tariffs on them."

About 62% of respondents said Trump's tariffs on Canada are bad for Michigan's economy, with 17% saying the tariffs are good. That split is especially pronounced among independent voters, who tend to play a major role in who wins and loses in Michigan elections and 70% of whom said the Canadian tariffs are bad for the state's economy.

Nearly 72% of the likely Michigan voters said the Canadian tariffs would cause an increase in what they pay for goods, according to the poll results.

Some elected Republicans in Michigan have expressed a desire for the Trump administration and Canadian officials to resolve the trade conflict, but they have stopped short of criticizing the president directly.

Republican U.S. Rep. John James, who is running for governor, in an Oct. 6 debate said he's called the Trump administration, specifically talking with the trade ambassador "and saying that we must get back to the table, stop acting like children, and negotiate a reciprocal, fair, and mutually beneficial arrangement to make sure that we can bring our jobs back and protect our industry."

U.S. House hopeful Michael Bouchard of Rochester Hills, a Republican running for James' vacant 10th District seat, said he'd like to see Trump's tariffs on Canadian imports end.

"I don't think our trade conflict with Canada is where we should be focusing a lot of our effort," Bouchard said Oct. 7 in an interview on The Detroit News' Political Insider podcast. "Everybody in Michigan knows Canadians. They're friends with Canada. It's 30 minutes from here to Canada."

Bouchard distinguished his remarks on Canadian tariffs from his support for Trump's global tariffs against China and other countries that are needed to "make sure that Americans are put in a position to succeed.

"But this tariffs on Canada stuff, I've been pretty blunt about that from the beginning," Bouchard said.

GOP U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett of Charlotte, who is locked in a tough reelection fight in his mid-Michigan district, told CNN on Sept. 9 that he's advocating for "cooler heads to prevail" in what he called a "tit for tat" back-and-forth between the U.S. and Canada.

"I want to see us get to a point where we can have mutually beneficial trade arrangements with Canada," Barrett said.

"I'm still hopeful that we'll get there, but that has been my advocacy ― both publicly and behind the scenes ― so that we can move in that direction. And I think it's going to take movement by both sides, the United States and Canada, to get to a mutual arrangement."

The former state lawmaker suggested on CNN that tariffs should be narrowly tailored to balance "anomalies" within U.S. trade arrangements. Barrett pointed to Canada's long-standing tariffs on U.S. dairy products, a policy designed to protect its country's milk, cheese and butter producers from competition.

Barrett said dairy farmers in his district are struggling to make market margins "in no small part because Canada has really manipulated their market there."

U.S. Rep. John Moolenaar, a Caledonia Republican, said last month that he is hoping for an end to the ongoing U.S.-Canada trade dispute, calling some of the negotiations so far counterproductive.

"Unfortunately, what normally is a civil private negotiation working towards agreements has spilled into some name-calling and some things that haven't been as productive as I'd like," Moolenaar said during a telephone town hall on Sept. 1.

"Quite frankly, we've got some work ahead of us," Moolenaar added. "Canada is an important trading partner, and my goal is to see this resolved in a constructive way."

Want to comment on this story? Become a subscriber today. Click here.

This article originally appeared on The Detroit News: Rogers shifts gears, calls for end to Trump's 'tariff war' with Canada

title: GOP spends big to rescue Paxton as his complaints strain ties with party allies
description:
National Republicans have spent months trying to rescue Ken Paxton. He’s complicating that effort.
Tensions are brewing with some Republicans after POLITICO published Paxton’s closed-door comments that “D.C.” Republicans were largely controlling his race.
fullText:
National Republicans have spent months trying to rescue Ken Paxton. He's complicating that effort.

Tensions are brewing with some Republicans after POLITICO published Paxton's closed-door comments that "D.C." Republicans were largely controlling his race.

"He is welcome to raise his own money and say whatever he wants," said one Republican involved in the Paxton rescue effort, who like others in this article was granted anonymity to speak candidly. "In fact, if he did that, he'd probably be winning right now and we wouldn't need to spend all this money."

"This just seems like Paxton preparing to blame others for what might be one of the most embarrassing defeats in modern political history," said Carlos Curbelo, a former Florida GOP representative.

Senate Republicans and top operatives didn't want to be in this position in the first place. Many had warned that the Trump effort to unseat Sen. John Cornyn and back Paxton in the primary would cost Republicans hundreds of millions to drag Paxton across the finish line in the general election. Cornyn and Senate GOP groups spent millions of dollars on ads during the primary attacking Paxton over his series of scandals and warning he was a flawed candidate.

Since then, the usual crowd of never-Paxton types has expanded into a wider circle of frustrated Republicans who are irked by the effort it's taking to boost the scandal-plagued Senate candidate. And Paxton saying he doesn't control his campaign messaging — alongside his remarks that President Donald Trump's midterm convention hurt him politically — isn't helping.

Paxton also complained about the drag of the Iran war and high prices on his campaign in another closed-door recording that Axios published Wednesday.

"Beggars can't be choosers. He can try to raise federal money at a level that is necessary to save his candidacy at this point but his arms don't reach that high," said a Texas-based GOP consultant who's closely monitoring multiple races. "As usual, he communicates something that is unhelpful, that is undisciplined, that is politically self-harmful and like most things, lacks any gratitude whatsoever."

The top Senate GOP super PAC, Trump's aligned MAGA Inc. operation and other Republicans are pumping more than $200 million into the race to salvage Paxton's campaign against Democrat James Talarico. Trump allies say they have worked hard to shore up Paxton, suggesting they've pushed donations toward the campaign and the larger GOP super PAC effort to avoid disaster in the Lone Star State. Trump plans to travel to Texas for the second time Wednesday to boost Paxton.

Paxton allies have brushed off his latest closed-door comments, saying he was referring to GOP super PACs he's not allowed to coordinate with as a candidate.

The Paxton campaign did not respond to a request for comment, though campaign adviser Nick Maddux said in response to POLITICO's initial report of the audio that "AG Paxton is thankful for the support and knows how important Texas is to keeping the majority, which is why he's on the ground every day."

But another Republican, a Trump ally working on the fundraising effort, said the national intervention isn't overstepping. That person said the messaging guidance from the national GOP is standard for major Senate races and that Paxton "needs the help."

One national GOP operative involved in the Texas Senate race noted that the attorney general's lackluster fundraising early on left him vulnerable to Talarico's attacks throughout the summer — especially over Paxton's series of "self-inflicted" scandals, which have made him "toxic" with key voting blocs in the deep red state.

"We warned them about this," the GOP operative said.

The Texas Senate race has sucked up oxygen, despite Trump winning the state in 2024 by double digits. And, the Senate map has kept expanding as Democrats have made gains in other typically red states, forcing Republicans to make critical decisions about where to allocate resources.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune and Republicans have said there are dedicated donors who are backing their effort to help Paxton, as they also try to shore up red seats across the map.

Paxton, in the September meeting with donors, acknowledged Washington's influence.

"I've never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign … it's all coming — you know — from D.C.," Paxton told donors during a small fundraising event last month, according to the audio.

Top GOP officials have tried to downplay Paxton's comments. The White House referred POLITICO to the RNC when asked for comment. The RNC argued Paxton, in the audio, was referring to the super PACs he can't coordinate with as a candidate.

"This is fake news nonsense mixed with lazy reporting demonstrating a clear ignorance about how super PACs work. President Trump has called Ken Paxton the single greatest attorney general in history and has been clear he will do whatever it takes to make him the next senator from Texas," RNC spokesperson Zach Kraft said in a statement.

Trump, when speaking to reporters at the White House on Tuesday, said he hadn't seen Paxton's latest comments. He added that his midterm travel blitz has helped Paxton and other Republican candidates.

"Ken's doing much better now that I — everybody is — since starting three, four days ago, since starting the rallies. It's brought a whole new awareness to how great the Republicans are doing, how great the economy is doing," Trump said, touting investments and manufacturing.

The president last week traveled to Texas and told the crowd that Paxton is a "pain in the ass sometimes" and later acknowledged he's "a little controversial." But, he also warned the Texas crowd that Talarico would be "such a horror to your state," adding, "we need the votes and I'm here for that, and I think we're going to win."

Vance also traveled to Texas, where he called Paxton an "amazing attorney general and your next senator."

Still, other Republicans have simply grown resigned to the state of the race, with Paxton needing all the aid he can get.

"There is only so much we can do," one senior Senate GOP aide said. "And I feel like we're doing a lot."

The Paxton campaign told POLITICO it raised $18 million in the third quarter across the campaign and his joint fundraising committees. That's roughly double his second-quarter total, though the campaign did not provide its cash-on-hand numbers, and Talarico has yet to release his fundraising haul.

Paxton also announced a $20 million ad buy last week — a significant single media investment in the race. But he's had to rely heavily on Trump, MAGA Inc. and the top Senate GOP super PAC to bail him out.

Republicans have largely leaned on the Senate Leadership Fund, rather than the Trump-aligned MAGA Inc. super PAC, to keep Paxton afloat. SLF is spending a Texas record-breaking $131 million sum through Oct. 12 and has pledged to continue to spend more through the final weeks of the election.

MAGA Inc. is increasing some spending for Paxton and is expected to hit near $45 million by Oct. 12.

If Paxton were to lose, Trump's reaction and whether he chooses to distance himself from the rescue effort will be driven by media coverage, said a former Trump fundraiser.

"If the media coverage related to election night and the autopsy a couple days afterwards is brutal towards Trump, like, horrible economy, inflation's not that much better than the last year of Joe Biden's ... he will lash out," the person said. "But if the narrative is, it's a midterm presidential, this is what normally happens … he'll move on as fast as he can and never talk about Ken Paxton again. It just depends what the coverage looks like post the November election."

Myah Ward contributed to this report.

title: Christa Pike is 'angry and confused' and can't move her arms after failed execution
description:
Christa Pike is feeling "angry and confused" after waking up in the hospital in the wake of a failed execution attempt that left her with severe physical health challenges that put her on a "long road to recovery," her attorneys said on Wednesday. 
Pike had been unconscious and in critical condition in the days after two doses of pentobarbital failed to end her life on Sept. 30, they said. 
"On Monday night, it was our understanding that Christa was brain-dead and that life support would be removed the next day," Randy Spivey, a member of her legal team, said during a press conference Wednesday afternoon. "But on Tuesday, to the shock of everyone … Christa woke up and began talking.
fullText:
Christa Pike is feeling "angry and confused" after waking up in the hospital in the wake of a failed execution attempt that left her with severe physical health challenges that put her on a "long road to recovery," her attorneys said on Wednesday.

Pike had been unconscious and in critical condition in the days after two doses of pentobarbital failed to end her life on Sept. 30, they said.

"On Monday night, it was our understanding that Christa was brain-dead and that life support would be removed the next day," Randy Spivey, a member of her legal team, said during a press conference Wednesday afternoon. "But on Tuesday, to the shock of everyone … Christa woke up and began talking."

Spivey said the effects of the pentobarbital have caused her to develop a blood clot, pneumonia and left her arms and hands "tremendously swollen," to the point where she's not currently able to use them. He added that Pike is still dealing with significant "cognitive confusion," but is "very aware" that the state had tried and failed to end her life.

The press conference came shortly after a hearing in which a judge granted Pike's attorneys' request to order the state to preserve all evidence connected to the execution, including medical equipment, communications related to the decision to call off the procedure or related to her emergency care and "anything that was in the actual room." The judge also ordered that any "barriers" that may prevent Pike from communicating with her attorneys while she's in the hospital be removed.

Pike's lawyers have repeatedly asked for Pike's death sentence to be commuted. During Wednesday's hearing, a lawyer representing the state declined to answer when asked whether Tennessee might attempt to execute Pike for a second time in the future.

Dr. Joel Zivot, a medical expert who has consulted with Pike's legal team, told the Associated Press on Tuesday that Pike's regaining consciousness "bodes well for a good recovery," but said that the full picture of her long-term health won't be clear for some time.

"She has recovered to a certain degree that she's able to be off a ventilator and able to speak, but in no way would I announce her free of further serious risk," he said. "There's still a lot of bad things that can happen here."

Fallout from the failed execution has brought intense scrutiny to Tennessee's execution procedures. Gov. Bill Lee suspended the one remaining execution scheduled for this year and announced that the state's top prison official, Correction Commissioner Frank Strada, would be stepping down at the end of October.

Pike's lawyers said the resignation was "justified, but it does nothing to help Christa now. What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person," they said in a statement, according to ABC News.

Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of her classmate, Colleen Slemmer. Her execution was scheduled to be carried out after 30 years on death row, but was called off after the drugs she was administered did not kill her. She was taken to the hospital, where she received life-saving care.

Both of Pike's arms were "swollen, burned, and blistered" when she arrived at the hospital, her lawyers wrote in a legal filing. Her lawyers believe the IV lines were placed incorrectly or her veins burst, so that some or all of the drug went into the tissue of her arms instead of her bloodstream.

"It was cruel, and it was torturous," attorney Randy Spivey said the day after the execution attempt. "It was also predictable."

Spivey said Pike's legal team warned the state of Tennessee and the courts that her medical condition of thrombocytosis "would cause her to suffer an agonizing death." They said it could increase clotting and pain during the execution process and that her veins are difficult to access. Pike's attorneys said the state and the court dismissed their client's concerns.

In audio recordings obtained by the New York Times, Pike had said two weeks before she was due to be executed that she was concerned about the lethal injection, citing a recent botched execution attempt in Tennessee of Tony Carruthers in May, when staff were unable to locate a vein. "Tony Carruthers lived out my worst nightmare," Pike can be heard saying in the audio, which was shared by her lawyers.

"I do not have good veins,' she said. "And I don't want to go through that."

"She was not seeking to delay her execution," attorney Stephen Ferrell told reporters on Oct. 1. "She was seeking to have that execution performed humanely and as quickly and as painlessly as possible."

Following the failed execution, Lee ordered "a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred" and said that another execution scheduled for Dec. 3 later this year had been paused.

"This is a tragedy," he said. "There is no one who wanted what happened last night to happen. It's deeply disturbing to me that this has happened in this state."

Pike's attorneys said in response that the governor's independent review doesn't go far enough after being in solitary confinement for more than 20 years and the botched execution attempt. "Christa has endured punishment greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty," Spivey said. "The governor must commute Christa's sentence now.

May Martinez, the mother of Pike's victim, Colleen Slemmer, told NBC News the execution attempt had been a "mess," adding, "They didn't say anything, and then, all of a sudden, they asked all the victims to leave. We didn't know anything until we got up to the office and saw the commissioner. And he said that it didn't work ... and she's on her way to the hospital."

U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the state's Republican candidate for governor, said Tennessee should look at other forms of execution. "If it's lethal injection, if it is electric chair, what we do know is we have to find a way to do this — and do it successfully," she told The Associated Press.

Tennessee officials have not said whether they will try to execute Pike again, or explained what went wrong.

Her condition could complicate any future attempt. Under Supreme Court precedent, a person can't be executed unless they have a "rational understanding" of why they are being put to death, the New York Times reported. Dr. Joel Zivot, an Emory University anesthesiologist retained by Pike's defense team, told the BBC it is "very possible" she suffered a brain injury because resuscitation was delayed.

Pike's lawyers have asked Lee to commute her sentence to life in prison. Lee had denied her clemency before the execution attempt.

President Trump questioned how the execution could have failed, telling reporters it "shouldn't be very difficult," according to AFP. United Nations human rights chief Volker Türk urged Tennessee not to try again.

Pike had been scheduled for execution at 10 a.m. Wednesday for killing Slemmer in 1995, at the age of 18. She would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.

An appeals court stopped the lethal injection just an hour before it was to start, a stay that was subsequently overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court.

Media witnesses said officials raised the curtains to the execution chamber at 7:27 p.m., showing Pike strapped to a gurney. "I'm going to leave this world the way I spent most of my life, and that is in love," she said in her "last" words.

However, Pike remained conscious after the first dose. Nashville Banner reporter Steven Hale said she lifted her head off the gurney at 7:54 p.m. She also reportedly asked prison officials if her arm was supposed to feel that way.

Tori Gessner, a journalist with WKRN News 2 in Nashville, said Pike was seen pointing at her arm and asking, "Does this happen like that?"

Pike continued to be heard snoring behind the closed curtain until the microphone was cut off at 8:53 p.m. At that time, an announcement was made to escort media witnesses out of the area.

Pike's legal team said in a statement to the Tennessean newspaper on Wednesday night, "We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy."

Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said what Pike experienced was "singular and unparalleled."

Seven other people have survived medical problems caused by an execution team's failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but no one has remained alive after receiving the drugs used in such executions, she said.

"I've witnessed, I believe, five executions in Tennessee," Gessner said. "Nothing about today was normal, typical at all, and the court delay was just the tip of the iceberg."

A source told NBC News that there was no medical oxygen or mask in the execution chamber, meaning they had to be brought in from a prison clinic. Some of the medication had worn off by the third time staff checked on Pike, the source added.

The Tennessee Department of Correction said that it "followed every step of the state's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the attorney general's office."

The state's execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered "if the inmate is not deceased" after the first set. It does not specify what happens if the subject is still alive after the second set.

Lawyers for Pike filed an emergency motion late Wednesday with the Tennessee Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution, saying she was in "unnecessary agony" and that the execution was violating her right to be free from cruel and unusual punishment. They also filed motions in the Sixth Circuit and a district court.

Pike was sentenced to death in 1996 after being convicted of first-degree murder of Colleen Slemmer the previous year on the University of Tennessee Agricultural campus.

According to legal documents filed with the Supreme Court, Pike "tortured, and killed Colleen Slemmer" on Jan. 12, 1995 because Pike "just felt mean that day." Pike is reported to have cut Colleen's throat multiple times and crushed her skull with a piece of asphalt.

Pike was also convicted of attempted first-degree murder after trying to strangle fellow inmate Patricia Jones in 2001.

According to the Death Penalty Information Center (DPIC), there were 75 botched lethal injections between 1982 and 2010. Compared to other methods, lethal injections face complications at a significantly higher rate. There have been a number of botched executions since 2010 that don't appear in the DPIC's tally.

Most of these were executions that went wrong in some way, but still ended in death. But there are seven known instances in which an execution failed entirely. One of them was earlier this year in Tennessee, when staff were unable to find a vein to administer the lethal drugs to inmate Tony Carruthers.

More than 20 pharmaceutical companies have also refused to have their products used in executions, which has left states struggling to find the drugs they need to perform lethal injections. In some cases, they have experimented with unproven alternatives, with disastrous results.

An Oklahoma prisoner named Michael Lee Wilson said he could feel his "whole body burning" as he was being executed using a controversial drug cocktail in 2014. There have also been instances of prisoners gasping for air, heaving and coughing, convulsing and being subjected to "three hours of pain" before finally dying.

In April 2022, Tennessee called off the execution of Oscar Smith about an hour before it was scheduled to begin after the state discovered that its lethal injection drugs had not been properly tested. An independent investigation found that the state had repeatedly failed to follow its own drug-testing protocols between 2018 and 2022.

Tennessee then revised its protocol, resuming executions in May 2025 and using a single, lethal drug: pentobarbital.

There's also growing evidence that lethal injection may not provide a peaceful death even when everything appears to go right.

Difficulties with lethal injections have led some states to revive previously discarded execution methods. South Carolina carried out three executions by firing squad last year. There had been three total firing squad executions in the U.S. in the previous half-century combined.

There were 47 executions in 2025, according to the DPIC, higher than the recent average of fewer than 30 per year. These included the lethal injection of South Carolina inmate Marion Bowman, who received twice the intended drug dose, and Tennessee inmate Byron Black, who reportedly showed sustained cardiac activity for nearly two minutes after prison staff pronounced him dead.

title: The Fed was unanimous about raising rates in September. Things have since changed.
description:
Minutes from the Federal Reserve's September policy meeting reflect unanimous agreement among officials that interest rates needed to be higher to combat persistent inflation.
"Participants generally emphasized that inflation remained elevated while the labor market appeared to be near full employment, with some signs of strengthening, and that economic activity was expanding at a solid pace. Furthermore, almost all participants assessed that, while inflation risks were tilted to the upside, risks to the labor market had diminished and were now broadly balanced," minutes from the Sept. 16 meeting released Wednesday stated. 
"Based on the outlook and the changing balance of risks, all participants viewed a higher target range for the federal funds rate as appropriate.
fullText:
Minutes from the Federal Reserve's September policy meeting reflect unanimous agreement among officials that interest rates needed to be higher to combat persistent inflation.

"Participants generally emphasized that inflation remained elevated while the labor market appeared to be near full employment, with some signs of strengthening, and that economic activity was expanding at a solid pace. Furthermore, almost all participants assessed that, while inflation risks were tilted to the upside, risks to the labor market had diminished and were now broadly balanced," minutes from the Sept. 16 meeting released Wednesday stated.

"Based on the outlook and the changing balance of risks, all participants viewed a higher target range for the federal funds rate as appropriate."

The Fed voted unanimously on Sept. 16 to raise rates, the first hike in three years. And at the time, most Federal Open Market Committee members saw a need for at least one more 25 basis point rate hike this year.

Markets were banking on a hike and expecting more to come.

But economic data released in the past few weeks has changed the picture considerably. "Core" PCE, the Fed's preferred inflation measure, rose a relatively cool 3% in August, beating expectations for a rise of 3.3% and marking a drop from 3.3% in July. Meanwhile, September jobs numbers fell far short of economists' expectations, with a gain of just 29,000 jobs, while the unemployment rate edged up to 4.2% from 4.1%.

That less rosy jobs picture, combined with a more positive read on inflation, had analysts — and some Fed officials — throwing cold water on the notion of another rate hike this month.

"This data won't shift the broader decision-making calculus for the Fed as inflation remains the supreme concern," Chris Hodge, chief economist for Natixis, previously told Yahoo Finance. "But with wages lower and the jobs picture a bit less rosy, it certainly decreases the urgency to hike in October (and perhaps December if inflation data cooperates)."

Even before the September job report, Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed president John Williams had already begun to temper expectations for a rate hike later this month. Both struck a more cautious tone than several of their colleagues, acknowledging that inflation has remained too high, but that the central bank should take time to assess whether it's on a downward path.

Williams said that, after raising rates in September, he sees "no need for urgency" and that "we have time to gather more information."

title: Maduro and his wife expected to face new charges over alleged torture of Americans
description:
Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro at the Miraflores Presidential Palace in Caracas, on October 15, 2021. - Federico Parra/AFP/Getty Images
Prosecutors in New York are expected to bring new charges against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores over the alleged torture of Americans who were held in Venezuelan government custody in recent years, according to multiple people familiar with the investigation.
An announcement could come as soon as Thursday, the people said.
The new charges relate to what the US government has said was the wrongful detention of more than a dozen US citizens in Venezuelan prisons during the time Maduro led a repressive regime in Venezuela, the people briefed on the investigation said.
Investigators have also discussed charging several additional people for their alleged role in the torture of Americans, according to a source familiar with the matter.
fullText:
Prosecutors in New York are expected to bring new charges against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores over the alleged torture of Americans who were held in Venezuelan government custody in recent years, according to multiple people familiar with the investigation.

An announcement could come as soon as Thursday, the people said.

The new charges relate to what the US government has said was the wrongful detention of more than a dozen US citizens in Venezuelan prisons during the time Maduro led a repressive regime in Venezuela, the people briefed on the investigation said.

Investigators have also discussed charging several additional people for their alleged role in the torture of Americans, according to a source familiar with the matter.

CNN has reached out to lawyers for Maduro and Flores.

Maduro and his wife were captured in a US military raid in January from the presidential palace in Caracas. They have pleaded not guilty to narcoterrorism conspiracy and other charges and are held without bail in New York.

Flores is expected to appear at a hearing Thursday where her lawyer will ask that she be moved to house arrest ahead of trial.

Maduro’s lawyer is challenging the legality of the arrest and argues the former president should have immunity since the alleged conduct occurred while he was in office.

The Venezuelan government is not joining in claiming immunity on his behalf, according to the prosecution.

More than a dozen Americans were detained by the Maduro government, which was accused by US government and advocates of using them as political pawns.

Several of the Americans have spoken out about the torture say they were subjected to while they were imprisoned. Matthew Heath and Osman Khan, who were freed in a prisoner swap in October 2022, alleged in a lawsuit that they were subjected to waterboarding, electrocution, threats of sexual assault, use of mind-altering drugs, and periods of solitary confinement. Heath, a US Marine veteran, attempted suicide while he was detained.

The “CITGO 6,” a group of six American oil executives who were lured to Venezuela in 2017 and detained for nearly five years, also say they were subjected to brutal conditions while in Venezuelan detention. In lawsuits filed against their employer — Citgo — Tomeu Vadell, Alirio Jose Zambrano and Jose Luis Zambrano said they were subjected to torture while imprisoned.

All of them had been held in the notorious General Directorate of Military Counterintelligence (DGCIM) — which was “responsible for arbitrary detentions, ill-treatment and torture of political opponents and their relatives,” according to a United Nations report.

That report found that DGCIM “routinely resorted” to torture practices “including electric shocks, suffocation with plastic bags, waterboarding, beatings, sexual violence, water and food deprivation, stress positions and exposure to extreme temperatures” in order to “extract information and confessions, intimidate, and punish the detainees.”

This story was updated with additional information.

title: Trump wants to turn his West Palm Beach golf course into the new Camp David
description:
Much of President Donald Trump’s second term has focused on changes to the nation’s capital.
But his ambitions to remake the physical architecture of the presidency transcend Washington: Trump wants to transform his West Palm Beach golf club into a presidential retreat modeled after Camp David.
Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. 
The plan calls for a parcel of the private club to be designated a permanent, official sanctuary for foreign leaders and future U.S.
fullText:
Much of President Donald Trump's second term has focused on changes to the nation's capital.

But his ambitions to remake the physical architecture of the presidency transcend Washington: Trump wants to transform his West Palm Beach golf club into a presidential retreat modeled after Camp David.

The plan calls for a parcel of the private club to be designated a permanent, official sanctuary for foreign leaders and future U.S. presidents, designed to host international summits and house presidents when they take vacations in Florida, according to a proposal presented to Palm Beach County officials by Trump International Golf Club's legal counsel. Future presidents would also be offered comped memberships to the Trump club.

"Just as Camp David, Windsor Castle, or the Elysee Palace are known worldwide, so too will the Presidential Golf Course in Palm Beach County," Harvey Oyer, a lawyer representing the Trump course, wrote to the Palm Beach County Board of County Commissioners in a letter last month. Oyer asked the county, which owns the property the course is on, to provide a piece of the land to the federal government, and he promised Trump would pay for the construction of a presidential residence and facilities on that land.

Oyer told The Washington Post that a name has yet not been selected for the presidential golf course.

"It would further cement Palm Beach County as one of the most recognizable brands and destinations in the world," Oyer said.

A spokesperson for the Trump Organization did not respond to requests for comment.

A White House official with knowledge of the proposed plans said in a text message the facilities would provide amenities of a "world-class property."

"The property is minutes away from the Donald J. Trump International Airport, does not have buildings looming, does not have houses along the course, has great security features, is close to law enforcement, and happens to be a highly rated golf course. These are features that are necessary for any presidential retreat," said the White House official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to preview plans.

In the letter, which was first reported by the Palm Beach Post, Oyer said the construction would not be completed before Trump leaves office, so the project would be "a gift" to Trump's successors and the county would benefit from high-power traffic in the area.

The county is seriously considering the proposal and is seeking more information, Palm Beach County Administrator Joseph Abruzzo told The Washington Post. In a meeting last week, Trump representatives assured county officials that, under the proposal, Trump's company would continue to make lease payments for the golf course and would agree to build the presidential retreat on a connected piece of land that would have a separate entrance from the private club, Abruzzo said.

Trump's club would continue to operate under the Trump family company and would probably benefit from more business if it becomes a site of long-lasting presidential importance.

The county is in contact with the General Services Administration, the agency that manages federal properties, and the county will be selecting a parcel of the land for the proposal, Abruzzo said.

"My understanding is that President Trump views this as a lasting contribution to the presidency and to those who will hold the office after him," Abruzzo said.

Though presidents already have a retreat at Camp David, Trump has visited the complex less frequently than many of his predecessors, preferring to spend his weekends and holidays at his own properties. He once commented that Camp David's rustic charm would wear off after half an hour.

Previous presidents have left their own marks on the woodsy Maryland retreat. Franklin D. Roosevelt established the getaway for federal workers as a presidential compound and dubbed it Shangri-La, though Dwight D. Eisenhower later named it after his father and grandson.

Marjorie Merriweather Post, who was once the wealthiest woman in the United States, also had hoped to create a presidential retreat in the South. She gifted her Palm Beach estate - better known as Mar-a-Lago - to the federal government upon her death in 1973, with the intention that it be turned into a Winter White House. But the National Park Service returned the property to her estate due to high maintenance costs, and Trump bought the property in 1985.

Trump International Golf Club opened in 1999 after Trump settled a lawsuit with the county regarding airplanes flying over Mar-a-Lago and the county agreed to lend him the land. Near the golf course, state officials have branded the Palm Beach airport and the road along it with Trump's name.

Trump's influence over Palm Beach and its image would be further cemented if the golf club becomes a presidential retreat. The wealthy strip of South Florida has undergone a MAGA transformation with Trump's base flocking to Mar-a-Lago for political events and networking. The nearby golf club has become a go-to destination for Trump spotting.

Trump reported an income of nearly $37 million last year from the golf course in his latest financial disclosure.

Although Trump had mocked former president Barack Obama for golfing during his presidency, Trump has frequently golfed since he has been in office. One online tracker calculated that Trump has spent at least 137 days in his second term golfing.

Rick Reilly, a former Sports Illustrated columnist who wrote "Commander in Cheat: How Golf Explains Trump," has golfed with Trump and said the president is less interested in the sport than the attention he gains at his own clubs. Reilly described how Trump always plays first in his golfing party and speeds on his golf cart to the next hole, wrapping up his game in less time than is typical, before heading to the clubhouse, where he makes the rounds, talking to his members and fans. If the Palm Beach club were a destination for foreign leaders, they would be part of the display of influence.

"I suppose he wants to make a power play with these people and show them who is the king of America," Reilly said.

Don Van Natta Jr., an ESPN senior writer who wrote "First Off the Tee: Presidential Hackers, Duffers, and Cheaters From Taft to Bush," a book on the history of presidents who golfed, said 17 of the past 20 presidents have golfed. The first avid golfer in the Oval Office was William Howard Taft, and the last president who didn't golf was Jimmy Carter.

"There is a long history of presidents playing golf," Van Natta said. "It's an escape where they can, as President [Bill] Clinton told me for my book, to be out in nature, and it's an escape hatch from the pressures of the Oval Office."

CORRECTION: A photo caption with a previous version of this article and on the homepage omitted the year that President Donald Trump arrived at Trump International Golf Club to watch the Super Bowl. It was in 2017.

fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has given the crew of the USS Abraham Lincoln a high-level award during a visit to the aircraft carrier Wednesday, a day before the ship returns home to San Diego after a record-long deployment in support of the Iran war.

The Presidential Unit Citation, the highest honor a unit can receive that is typically reserved for significant achievement in combat, was bestowed upon the Lincoln and accompanying ships for "40 days of combat operations and an ironclad maritime blockade against Iran in support of Operation Epic Fury," Hegseth said, referring to the Trump administration's code name for the Iran war.

The carrier endured a record 265 uninterrupted days at sea, and its extended deployment drew national attention following reports of crew stress and poor mental health, as well as supply shortages, including food and hygiene products. After more than 10 months deployed, the Lincoln's crew got a stop in Thailand early last month on the way back from the Middle East.

Hegseth, who flew out to the ship before its arrival Thursday in San Diego, acknowledged to the crew that "I'm the only thing standing between you and home" and that his intention was "once they pull up to the dock, we're getting out of the way."

Long deployments can tax service members who are away from their families for extended periods while facing threats, and can add wear to the aircraft carriers, which have been used for President Donald Trump's military operations in the Middle East and South America.

The Lincoln is the second carrier that has endured an unusually long and arduous deployment to support the war against Iran and the second to receive the top unit award afterward.

Hegseth in May met the crew of the USS Gerald R. Ford during its return from a 326-day deployment — the longest for an aircraft carrier in the past 50 years and a record in the post-Vietnam War era.

As for the Lincoln, it departed San Diego in late November, arrived in the Middle East in January and now will be back in its home port.

Hegseth said Wednesday that Trump "tracked your activities from day one and couldn't be more proud of what you executed."

The Navy initially played down early reports of supply problems on Lincoln and Trump said its lengthy deployment was "not nearly long enough," Navy leaders, however, eventually acknowledged there were some issues aboard.

In August, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the Lincoln maintained adequate food supplies, but because combat operations limited resupply opportunities, meal options were reduced from two to one for a short time. He said in a letter to a Democratic lawmaker seeking information that four nutritionally balanced meals were served daily.

Navy officials also said that while combat operations led to delays in scheduled resupply shipments, they prioritized the delivery of hygiene products and established a rotation to streamline distribution to different squadrons.

More recently, the service told lawmakers that eight sailors attempted suicide while on the long deployment. Experts say that number is low in a strike group of 6,000 sailors over 10 months.

Hegseth pushed back against what he said were efforts to turn the "Lincoln into some sort of a symbol, a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission."

He said that "what makes the U.S. military and the U.S. Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you're resilient and you overcome — you finish the mission nonetheless."

According to the award that Hegseth read to the crew, the Lincoln and the strike group executed 3,693 combat missions, delivered 1.37 million pounds of ordnance, launched 450 Tomahawk cruise missiles, shot down 77 one-way attack drones, sank 64 Iranian warships, destroyed 21 anti-ship cruise missiles and defended against four fast attack craft and explosive-carrying ships.

There are now two aircraft carriers assigned to the Middle East. The USS George Washington, though usually based in Asia, relieved the Lincoln in August.

The other aircraft carrier, the USS George H.W. Bush, has been deployed for about six months, but it pulled into Phuket, Thailand, for a port visit several days ago.

U.S. officials have said a third aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, and thousands of troops aboard it and accompanying ships could join the Washington and the Bush as early as the end of October.

title: Amazon's New 'About You' Page Lists Everything It Knows About You
description: You can now see—and shape—what Amazon knows about you.
fullText:
It shouldn't come as a surprise that Amazon collects data about you based on what you buy. And now, you can get a direct look at what the company has concluded from all that activity.

Amazon's "About You" page, currently in beta after launching this May, uses data from customers' activity to generate details about them in categories like Product Preferences, Interests & Hobbies, and Home & Family. Amazon uses those details to personalize the shopping experience. Here's how to navigate and personalize your "About You" page in your Amazon account.

The results can be oddly specific. My editor-in-chief, Jordan Calhoun, shared his page, which includes these entries:

"Prioritizes plant-based meat alternatives over traditional options"

"Subscribes to multiple streaming services continually"

Full disclosure: I try to never use Amazon personally. I pretty much exclusively use it to round up deals for you, my dear reader. That being said, here's what Amazon thinks it knows about me: "Values durable travel gear," "prefers athletic and casual clothing styles," "practices yoga regularly," and "listens to music frequently."

In its Privacy Notice, Amazon lists every activity that provides user data to the company. That includes the obvious, like searching for items and placing orders. It also includes actions you may not realize are being tracked, like interacting with Alexa Voice Service, participating in discussion boards, or linking an Amazon account to a third-party business.

Hover over where Amazon says "Hello, [your name]" in the upper right corner.

Under the "Your Account" section, click "Account."

Under the "Ordering and shopping preferences" section, click "Your Shopping preferences."

From here, you can add information of your own, like your shoe size, interests, and dietary preferences. Scroll to the bottom of the page, and you'll see a blue hyperlinked option that says, "Manage your information." Click it, and you'll see what dirt Amazon has on you.

Tap the hamburger icon in the bottom menu bar, then go to Account > Shopping preferences > About you.

Shoppers can't directly opt out of the "About you" feature. They can, however, customize the data by adding details they want Amazon to know and deleting assumptions they consider inaccurate or too personal.

On the "About you" page, customers also have the option to "make Amazon even more personal to you" by importing personal data they've shared with other AI agents. Amazon provides a prompt for you to feed to your chatbot to generate a shopping profile, then asks you to copy the bot's response and paste it back into Amazon.

Whether that's worth doing is up to you. Given how much Amazon already infers from your browsing and buying, handing over a profile from another AI service is a choice worth thinking through. Either way, taking a few minutes to review your page and delete anything inaccurate or too personal is a simple way to see and shape what Amazon knows about you.

title: Democrats allege Trump allies benefited from a $1.7 billion Balkan gas deal
description:
London — The involvement of a small American firm linked to associates of President Trump in an energy project in Bosnia and Herzegovina worth more than $1.5 billion has raised questions about how the White House could be using its leverage in the fragile Balkan state.
U.S. lawmakers accuse the Trump administration of lifting sanctions on Bosnian Serb separatist leader Milorad Dodik in an effort to enrich and empower allies of Mr.
fullText:
London — The involvement of a small American firm linked to associates of President Trump in an energy project in Bosnia and Herzegovina worth more than $1.5 billion has raised questions about how the White House could be using its leverage in the fragile Balkan state.

U.S. lawmakers accuse the Trump administration of lifting sanctions on Bosnian Serb separatist leader Milorad Dodik in an effort to enrich and empower allies of Mr. Trump, and of undermining longstanding U.S. foreign policy interests in the region in the process.

On Sunday, Mr. Trump was hailed by Dodik after his Serb nationalist party won one of Bosnia and Herzegovina's three presidency seats, which are split between Bosnia's Muslim minority, known as Bosniaks, as well as Serb and Croat ethnic groups under the country's complex power-sharing electoral system.

"If it had not been for Donald Trump's magnificent victory … we would probably be political corpses today," Dodik told supporters in a speech, in which he also thanked Russian President Vladimir Putin for his support.

AAFS Infrastructure & Energy, a company incorporated in the U.S. last year and headed by President Trump's former personal attorney Jesse Binnall and Joseph Flynn, the brother of Trump ally General Michael Flynn, is close to securing a contract to develop the Southern Interconnection Gas Pipeline.

The pipeline project has been discussed by Bosnian officials for years, but long opposed by Dodik, who has close ties with the Kremlin. But Dodik, whose party has veto power in Bosnia's parliament, said he would not stand in the way of the proposal following the announcement of AAFS' involvement last April. Six months earlier, the Trump administration lifted sanctions against Dodik that were imposed by the U.S. Treasury almost a decade ago.

The pipeline would connect Bosnia and Herzegovina to Croatia's gas network, allowing Bosnia to import liquefied natural gas (LNG) from its neighbors. The project, which is valued at around $1.7 billion according to the Croatian government, would help make Bosnia and Herzegovina less reliant on Russian gas imports.

On its website, AAFS describes itself as a company focused on "energy security, project structuring, capital alignment, and long-term regional infrastructure development."

The company does not appear to have demonstrable experience in any similar energy projects.

The secessionist leader Dodik, who until recently served as the president of Bosnia's self-governing, Serb-run territory called Republika Srpska, has long been accused of undermining the U.S. brokered Dayton Accords, which ended the bloody sectarian violence between Bosnia, Croatia and Serbia in the 1990s.

The sanctions, which included asset freezes and visa bans, were imposed by the Obama administration in 2017. The Biden administration then imposed further sanctions in 2022, accusing Dodik of corruption, including the charge that he had handed government contracts to close business associates in Republika Srpska.

A congressional report published last month by House Democrats, titled "Pay for Play in the Balkans," alleges that those two decisions — the removal of sanctions on Dodik and his decision to not oppose the pipeline — are directly linked.

"The Trump administration has used its diplomatic influence and connections with shady characters like Michael Flynn … to facilitate the concession contract for the SIC [Southern Interconnection Gas pipeline] to AAFS Infrastructure and Energy LLC, a company owned and operated by Michael Flynn's brother Joseph Flynn and Trump-affiliated lawyer and political activist Jesse Binnall," the report alleges.

AAFS Infrastructure and Energy LLC did not respond to a CBS News request for comment.

Foreign agent registration filings (FARA) cited in the report and reviewed by CBS News show that Michael Flynn, President Trump's former national security adviser, last worked as a paid lobbyist for Republika Srpska in October 2025, the month during which the sanctions against Dodik were lifted.

Those same filings show that Flynn was paid $100,000 for that work by RRB Strategies, a lobbying firm run by Rod Blagojevich, the former Illinois governor who was convicted in 2011 of 18 counts of corruption and spent nearly eight years in a federal prison before being pardoned by President Trump last year.

Flynn provided strategic advice and counsel, analysis and information research, and introductions to the Republika Srpska government, according to the FARA filings.

Blagoyevich's firm originally signed a contract to "provide communications and public affairs support on behalf of the Republic of Srpska" in March 2025, separate FARA filings reviewed by CBS News show.

CBS News sought comment from email aliases associated with Flynn and Blagojevich, but did not receive any response by the time of publication.

On Nov. 13, 2025, the U.S. Embassy in Sarajevo said in a social media post that Chargé d'Affaires John Ginkel had met Bosnian Prime Minister Nermin Niksic to discuss the gas pipeline project and "to support the importation of U.S. gas through Croatia to consumers in Bosnia and Herzegovina."

One week later, the embassy announced a preliminary agreement for an "American company to develop, build, and manage the pipeline."

Four days after that, on Nov. 24, AAFS Infrastructure & Energy was incorporated in the state of Wyoming.

In January, the U.S Embassy in Sarajevo posted again confirming that a meeting had taken place between AAFS leadership, including Joseph Flynn and Binnall, and top Bosnian officials.

AAFS was then granted the status of lead investor and operator on the proposed natural gas pipeline in legislation passed by Bosnia's parliament in April.

Later that month, the Croatian and Bosnian governments signed a contract to construct the pipeline with U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright in attendance for the signing ceremony. At a news conference with Bosnia's energy minister on April 2, Binnall hailed the pipeline project as a "priority" for the Trump administration.

The White House declined to comment on the pipeline project last week, but an administration official said the sanctions against Dodik were lifted to prevent instability in the Balkans.

"This is yet another example of President Trump's pragmatic, farseeing foreign policy that has prevented disasters on perennial issues that his predecessors so often stumbled into," a White House official told CBS News on Friday, without elaborating on the type of disasters the Trump administration was preventing.

A State Department letter published as part of the House Democrat-authored congressional report said the decision to delist Dodik had helped ensure peace and stability in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The official who wrote the letter, Paul Guaglianone, said lifting sanctions against Dodik had led to Bosnian Serb separatists rolling back policies that would have destabilized Bosnia's government.

The lifting of sanctions "advanced U.S. interests in [Bosnia and Herzegovina] and the Western Balkans. On October 18, the Republika Srpska National Assembly (RSNA) withdrew most of the anti-Dayton legislation it had passed in recent years," the letter read. That legislation had included laws that would have blocked Bosnia's national police and judiciary from having any authority in Republika Srpska.

Political scientist and Balkans foreign policy expert Jasmin Mujanović told CBS News the legislation in question had already been struck down prior to the lifting of the sanctions against Dodik, and he was skeptical of the Trump administration's justifications for the move.

"This package of omnibus secessionist laws that the Serb nationalist authorities and the RS [Republika Srpska] entity in Bosnia had unlawfully voted through in the local assembly had already been struck down by the Constitutional Court of Bosnia Herzegovina," he said.

"If the argument is that the Trump administration nevertheless managed to get Dodik and his people to withdraw the laws, it's still unclear what the significance of that is, or for that matter, why, given that the laws are moot," he said, adding that it would "result in sanctions relief for an entire regime."

title: Weeks before Election Day, the FEC can't enforce campaign finance law
description:
In July, Reps. Mike Lawler, a New York Republican, and Josh Gottheimer, a New Jersey Democrat, had a request for the Federal Election Commission: help make sure artificial intelligence chatbots do not feed voters false information about the 2026 midterm elections. 
The lawmakers, writing to the FEC as well as the Justice and Homeland Security departments, urged the agencies to coordinate on "AI-driven threats to election integrity" and to press AI companies on their safeguards. Their concerns come as a quarter of likely voters use AI tools daily and at least 38% have gotten information about candidates or voting from AI search summaries, according to a September survey released by the American Association of Political Consultants Foundation.
But later that month, FEC Commissioner Shana Broussard, a Democrat, wrote back with a blunt answer: the agency couldn't help.

title: 10 Shows Like 'Carrie' You Should Watch Next
description: High school is hell.
fullText:
Do we need another adaptation of Carrie? Maybe/maybe not, but the horrific bullying faced by the teen protagonist of Stephen King's first book is not even the tiniest bit less relevant now than it was way back in 1974, and Mike Flanagan has proven himself King's most adept modern-day translator—and that's before taking his other work into consideration. So we'll happily give it a shot before diving into these other shows to remind ourselves that growing up is hell.

There are at least a couple of different levels to The Glory, a justifiably well-received South Korean import, rather remarkably holding together despite some wild shifts in tone. Most obviously, it's a revenge drama, with a relatively simple set-up: Song Hye-kyo plays Moon Dong-eun, an elementary school homeroom teacher who's playing a very long game: Her school bullies are grown up now, and their kids (some of them, anyway) are now in Dong-eun's care. Right where she wants them. Smartly, the show makes clear the extent of the past violence faced by Dong-eun (much of it hard to watch), and the resulting post-traumatic stress that's consumed her life. The parents of her tormentors were all far too wealthy for the girls to face any consequences for their actions, so Dong-eun feels like she has no choice. It could have been a revenge fantasy, or a straight horror show about a woman carrying out a questionable revenge, but instead it's a more nuanced tale of high school bullying, with a victim whose revenge takes a much colder path than Carrie's. Stream The Glory on Netflix.

Sophia Lillis, straight from playing Beverly Marsh in the It movies (if you wanted a Stephen King connection), stars as Sydney Novak, a 17-year-old living in a small town with her mother and sister. Her father recently died by suicide; she has a crush on her best friend; and all she and her mother do is argue. In the middle of all of that, she discovers that she has powers triggered by her emotions, both of which she'll need to learn to control if she wants to get her life in order. As the lead, Lillis sells the hell out of this offbeat coming-of-age story—the tone is more dark comedy than horror, but Sophia definitely has some Carrie moments of her own before it's over. Stream I Am Not Okay With This on Netflix.

Situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (think Lost or Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii. It quickly becomes clear that the accident was engineered and that the whole thing is some sort of social experiment, and the survivors are forced to compete against each other if they want to live. The show understands the ways in which young women are exploited and expected to compete against each other in the real world, mirroring the horrors of the high school social hierarchy that dominate Carrie's life. Stream The Wilds on Prime Video.

Likely the least buzzy of Mike Flanagan's Netflix offerings, coming, as it did, near the end of his contract with the streamer, is every bit as good as the others. Based on the YA novel by Christopher Pike, it follows a group of eight terminally ill young patients at a bucolic hospice home run by a secretive and mysterious doctor (A Nightmare on Elm Street's Heather Langenkamp). Each night, the kids meet secretly to share scary stories, with each also promising to return from beyond the grave when the time comes. Spooky, funny, and impressively moving as a coming-of-age story about kids who know they'll never come of age, the show was planned as more than a miniseries, but the ending is still pretty satisfying. Stream The Midnight Club on Netflix.

Kathryn Newton heads this surprisingly smart William Golding/Lord of the Flies riff about a group of teenagers forced to create their own community after all the adults disappear and a dense new forest crops up around their small enclave, cutting them off from everything and everyone else. This one's about coming of age in a world where the usual rules are no longer in effect, and about how we're quick to reestablish an oppressive social order even when outside forces are no longer at work. Stream The Society on Netflix.

A cloistered, repressive upbringing for a young woman with dramatic telekinetic powers? The stories of Carrie and Eleven play out very differently, but that's largely because they're in different kinds of stories—one's a more introspective high school drama, while the other is a retro government conspiracy adventure involving demons and parallel universes. Still! You kinda feel like Carrie and El would recognize each other's trials, with hope that the bullied kids of Hawkins would welcome them both. You're probably familiar with Stranger Things by now, but just in case: An ensemble cast of mostly kids uncover dark deeds in their small Indiana town after a mysterious girl (Millie Bobby Brown) turns up displaying impressive, if alarming, abilities. Stream Stranger Things on Netflix.

The big link here is, of course, Stephen King, who's not just great at situating horror in small towns, but in conveying the unique trauma of being a kid trapped in a small town—Carrie and It being two of his best in that vein. Set in the 1960s, this It prequel dives into the backstory of Derry and Pennywise the clown through the eyes of children who met him during his previous visit to the town. By the end of the first episode, it's clear that even the most adorable children aren't safe, and this is a show that will, if nothing else, go hard—and that's before Bill Skarsgård's memorably creepy Pennywise even shows up, and before we dig deeper into the secrets and lies of the adults of Derry. As in the book and earlier adaptations, each kid here has their own specific family and social issues, and Pennywise is very good at exploiting those dynamics to make the kids feel isolated and afraid. Stream It: Welcome to Derry on HBO Max.

Hang in there, Carrie! Help is on the way! Well, OK...maybe if you lived in South Korea and in the very specific world of this webtoon adaptation. Following a rise in bullying, violence, and generally shitty behavior in high schools, including the murder of a teacher, the government establishes the Educational Rights Protection Bureau (ERPB)—tasked with reforming the school system BY ANY MEANS NECESSARY. The team's first assignment takes them to a school where a bullied student has recently died by suicide, strongly related to the actions of the son of a prominent politician. What else to do but expose dad's secrets, knocking the bully down a few pegs and leaving him vulnerable to the consequences of his own actions. It's a little less Carrie and a little more Avengers: High School, but it's a fun fantasy for anyone who had a rough time back then. Stream Teach You a Lesson on Netflix.

Mariam (Andria Tayeh) is brutally bullied by the cool clique at her private school in this Jordanian import, a high school drama that's both universal and distinctly Muslim in character. Fed up, Mariam convinces a couple of similarly outcast friends to join forces with her in a revenge plot that quickly gets out of hand. The show deals with Jordanian-style patriarchy head-on, without drawing any easy conclusions about its characters—Mariam catfishes one of her bullies and convinces her to send a revealing picture, one that she immediately posts, exploiting the very same repressive cultural elements that she claims to deplore. It's a smart and compelling drama with soapy elements (as well as a surprise hit for Netflix), and few if any clear heroes or villains. Stream AlRawabi School for Girls on Netflix.

One of our most reliable horror franchises went the series route with impressively smart results. Zackary Arthur is Jake Wheeler, a queer teen subject to relentless bullying at school and abuse at home from his homophobic father. Jake picks up America's favorite serial-killing doll at a garage sale school art project. Before long, Jake's tormentors are facing consequences rather a bit beyond what Jake would have hoped for, and he's torn between fighting Chucky or leaning into the chaos. The tone is very different, of course, but Chucky's violence plays out very much like an externalized (and quippier) manifestation of Carrie's abilities—both teens dealing with forces that they have little control over. Stream Chucky on Peacock and Prime Video.

title: Barry-Murphy and Bellamy 'so similar' - Lawlor
description: Cardiff boss Brian Barry-Murphy and Wales head coach Craig Bellamy have similar outlooks says Dylan Lawlor.
fullText:
Cardiff and Wales defender Dylan Lawlor says club boss Brian Barry-Murphy and national team head coach Craig Bellamy have similar outlooks.

Lawlor has become a key member of Barry-Murphy's Cardiff side which last season secured promotion to the Championship.

The 20-year-old was handed his first senior Wales cap by Bellamy in September 2025 and has made six appearances in the past year.

"They are so similar so it's easy to switch between the two," Lawlor said of playing for Barry-Murphy at Cardiff and under Bellamy for Wales.

"They're so detailed and see football the same way and to be honest it's the same way I see it.

"It suits me and it's easy to switch between the two."

Lawlor said both Barry-Murphy and Bellamy had the same approach to games as ex-Liverpool boss Jurgen Klopp.

Former Liverpool defender Andy Robertson said Klopp focused on their own strengths while predecessor Arne Slot would "constantly adapt to the opponent's tactics".

"The most eye-opening thing for me is that it's all about us," Lawlor told the BBC's Welsh language podcast, Y Coridor Ansicrwydd (Corridor of Uncertainty).

"I saw what Andy Robertson said about Slot and Klopp and the difference.

"It's obvious to me at Cardiff and for Wales that it's all about us and not to worry about the opposition.

"You go into games full of confidence – it's all about us."

Barry-Murphy was appointed Cardiff head coach in June 2025 following the club's relegation from the Championship at the end of the 2024-25 season.

Lawlor made his league debut in the final game of that season, coming on as a second-half substitute against Norwich City.

He was given his opportunity by interim boss Aaron Ramsey, a fellow former pupil at Lawlor's old school of Ysgol Cwm Rhymni in Caerphilly County.

"He was someone I could look up to," Lawlor said.

"He was an inspiration to me when I was growing up and then I had the chance to work with him and then under him when he was starting his coaching career.

"He would pass on things to me, tips and things I could add to my game and when it comes from someone like that you have to take it."

Lawlor missed pre-season and the start of the Championship campaign with a knee injury he picked up playing for Wales against Ghana in June.

He returned as a substitute Cardiff's Championship win over Charlton just before the recent international break, but that came too soon for involvement in Wales' four recent Nations League games.

"To be honest I wasn't in the picture to be part of the camp," Lawlor said.

"I think the most important thing for me is to focus on November and try and be fit for the games against Portugal and Norway.

Lawlor admits he was "gutted" to miss out on facing two of football's superstars in Portugal's Cristiano Ronaldo and Erling Haaland of Norway.

"Fingers crossed I will be able to play against them in November and prove myself against them," he added.
