title: 'Draining' few days for Gauff after online racist abuse
description: Coco Gauff says she had a "draining" few days after receiving racist abuse online before her fourth-round China Open exit.
fullText:
Coco Gauff said she had a "draining" few days after receiving racist abuse online before her fourth-round China Open exit.

The American received an "insane" amount of racist comments and direct messages following an incident in her third-round win over 16-year-old Sun Xinran on Monday.

China's Sun thought she had hit a winner late in the first set, but Gauff raised her hand to halt play because of a flickering light in the side panels surrounding the court.

After a video review - which players are allowed to request - the point was replayed, with Gauff winning it and subsequently going on to clinch the match.

The 22-year-old posted a lengthy statement explaining what had happened and later condemned the racist abuse she received in response.

Gauff was beaten 6-3 6-3 in her next match against Elise Mertens on Wednesday.

Asked how she had felt over the past 36 hours, Gauff said: "It has been kind of draining, I'm not going to lie.

"I just turn off my phone and move on. I mean, there's nothing you can do."

A spokesperson for the Women's Tennis Association said it was appalled by the abuse. It said it was in contact with Gauff "to offer our full support".

A statement given to the news agency AFP said the governing body was "seeking action" against the abusive content.

Gauff, who won the title in Beijing in 2024, committed 34 unforced errors and eight double faults against Mertens.

"I was just a bit flat. That's the main thing," Gauff said.

"The level was there at some points, I just didn't sustain it the whole match."

Belgium's Mertens will play former world number one Iga Swiatek in the quarter-finals after the six-time major champion Swiatek beat American teenager Iva Jovic 6-1 6-3.

title: Pidcock angry after team-mates hit by police vehicle
description: Tom Pidcock wanted to "stop racing" after he says two of his team-mates were hit by a police vehicle travelling the wrong way down the course at the Tre Valli Varesine.
fullText:
Tom Pidcock wanted to "stop racing" after saying that two of his team-mates were hit by a police vehicle travelling the wrong way down the course at the Tre Valli Varesine in Italy.

Pidcock finished second at the one-day race in Varese but was left "mad" after Pinarello-Q36.5 team-mates Marcel Camprubi and Thomas Gloag were knocked off their bikes with six laps of the finishing circuit to go.

Spain's Camprubi was able to continue in the race but Pidcock's fellow Briton Gloag stopped and required stitches on his knee.

"First of all, I wanted to stop the race, stop racing myself," Pidcock told Eurosport after the race, which was won by Belgium's Jarno Widar in a sprint finish.

"I was mad. I had guys all riding in front of me, for me, and then two of them are on the floor.

"This shouldn't happen. But we continued and got back into the race and I'm happy that I could be on the podium."

BBC Sport has contacted race organisers and local police for comment.

In August, two-time Olympic mountain bike champion Pidcock won his second cross-country world title at the Mountain Bike World Championships.

He dedicated that win to British cyclist Finlay Tarling, 19, who died on 14 August during the Volta a Portugal following a high-speed collision with a van that had strayed on to the closed road.

Camprubi posted a picture of a broken bike on Instagram Stories, with a caption that read: "Sad that you have to risk your life to race, one month after a tragic accident."

Pidcock replied saying: "These accidents must stop."

title: Arteta signs new contract with champions Arsenal
description: Mikel Arteta says this is "only the beginning" of Arsenal's success after signing a new contract with the Premier League champions until 2030.
fullText:
Manager Mikel Arteta says this is "only the beginning" of Arsenal's success after signing a new contract with the Premier League champions until 2030.

BBC Sport reported earlier this month that an agreement had been made on an improved new contract.

The Spaniard's deal was set to expire at the end of this season, with his time in charge of the Gunners now possibly stretching to a decade following his arrival in December 2019.

Atletico Madrid boss Diego Simeone is reportedly paid over £20m per year, as was former Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola - both of whom Arteta benchmarked his worth against.

The new contract includes an increase from his current salary of £10m per year plus an additional £5m in bonuses.

"This club is unique, its character and the way it makes you feel, and I have a great sense of privilege that our journey together will continue," Arteta said.

"We have already built a special bond and created memories that will last a lifetime, and what is so exciting is that this is only the beginning of what we can achieve together."

The 44-year-old has won a Premier League and FA Cup in charge of Arsenal, losing the Champions League final against Paris St-Germain in May.

News of Arteta's new deal at Arsenal won't come as a shock.

The fact his previous deal expired at the end of the season did put a slightly greater emphasis on the speed of discussions than normal.

But Arteta has been transparent about his desire to stay at the club beyond the end of this campaign.

Dynasty building is what has driven Arteta's decision. Winning Arsenal's first Premier League title in 20 years last season is viewed as just the start.

Coming within a penalty kick of winning their first Champions League trophy came as a gut-wrenching blow - but also a huge motivation.

"We share a special bond with Mikel. We are so proud of everything we have achieved since he returned to the club in 2019," co-chairmen Stan and Josh Kroenke said.

"He has a deep understanding of Arsenal's values and carries them in his heart. He knows what this club means to everyone connected to it and is committed to building on everything we have achieved together."

With that in mind, there was never a sense Arteta was preparing to walk away from the team he has built to become one of the best in European football.

So with a deal for their manager to stay now agreed, the foundation of Arsenal's recent revitalisation into a footballing force remains in place.

Does more history beckon? Arteta is committed to finding out.

title: Russell to start from back of Singapore grid after penalty
description: Britain's George Russell will start from the back of the grid in Sunday's Singapore Grand Prix because of a power-unit penalty from last weekend's race.
fullText:
Britain's George Russell will start from the back of the grid in Sunday's Singapore Grand Prix.

The Mercedes driver has received a power-unit penalty from a dramatic Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia last Sunday.

The 28-year-old qualified in eighth but was heading for a podium finish before an engine failure forced him to retire from third place with five laps remaining.

Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff has confirmed that Russell needs to take a new power unit this weekend, putting him over the limit on several components and meaning he will be penalised in Singapore.

Russell's retirement last Sunday meant Kimi Antonelli, who finished second behind Max Verstappen, took a big leap towards his first Formula 1 world title as the Italian is now 84 points ahead of his Mercedes team-mate.

There are six or seven races remaining, depending on whether F1 gets the security reassurances it needs for Qatar and Abu Dhabi, in the context of the war in the Middle East.

"[Russell's penalty] is particularly frustrating given the way he drove last weekend and the result he deserved to be fighting for," said Wolff.

"Unfortunately, these things are part of the sport and our focus now is on giving him the best possible car and opportunities to fight back through the field."

The engine penalty is a particularly large blow for Russell as overtaking is notoriously difficult in Singapore.

His title hopes are already effectively over with either six or seven races still o go, even if he still has a mathematical chance of catching Antonelli.

But it means his chances of cutting the Italian’s lead are drastically reduced, even if Antonelli runs into trouble.

Mercedes had no choice but to fit a new engine for Russell in Singapore because he had no usable engines remaining in his allocation.

After early season reliability problems, they were all either broken or too high on mileage.

Antonelli won the Italian Grand Prix last month having taken a similar penalty, while this is the latest setback in a season of frustrating mechanical issues for Russell, who won last year's Singapore Grand Prix.

Extra points are on offer this weekend as Singapore hosts the sixth and final sprint event of the season. Russell's penalty will apply to Sunday's Grand Prix and not the sprint race on Saturday.

"We have spent the days since [last Sunday] working hard to understand why our performance was not where it should have been," Wolff added.

"Singapore gives us an immediate opportunity to continue that work.

"We need to keep learning and score the strongest result we can with both cars."

title: Tuchel's England 2.0: what has changed?
description: What has Thomas Tuchel tweaked as he looks to refine his England blueprint rather than rewrite it from scratch?
fullText:
After the World Cup, Thomas Tuchel was asked whether he had seen his vision of England during the tournament - a question that drew a hesitant and unsure answer.

Over the summer, the Three Lions found ways to win but often leaned on scrappy moments of brilliance rather than methodical dominance.

Tuchel had in mind the type of team, the tactics and the patterns he wanted to see.

He and his assistant coach Anthony Barry have often spoken about borrowing ideas from the Premier League.

Building up short. Enticing pressure. Playing quickly across the middle of the pitch – whether through powerful carrying or long balls – to find runners in attack against fewer defenders.

These were all ideas England tried to execute, to varying levels of success, in the World Cup.

During the recent international break, many of the ideas we saw during the World Cup and prior have persisted.

There have, however, been deliberate changes in tactics and personnel, with the 53-year-old Tuchel looking to refine his blueprint rather than rewrite it from scratch.

England have continued to focus on first playing short from the back, intent on drawing opponents towards them before speeding up play to find their attackers in space.

Rather than giving the build-up responsibilities to two central defenders and a holding midfielder as they did during the World Cup, England have committed an extra player to this central build-up unit.

Two central midfielders and two central defenders look to solve problems against pressing attackers with a shape that fluctuates between a 2-2 or a 3-1.

Tuchel has praised Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott, who took turns with Myles Lewis-Skelly to pair with Elliot Anderson in the heart of midfield in Declan Rice's absence.

Either player taking the role of busy partner for Anderson - boasting technical quality and an ability to take turns playing as a lone holding midfielder - have proved successful for England.

Anderson, who sat at the base of midfield for much of the World Cup has, as a result, been deployed in a more varied role.

With Scott or Lewis-Skelly picking up the ball from the centre-backs, Anderson has dropped to form part of the back three alongside Marc Guehi and Ezri Konsa.

This has given him time and space on the ball, facing forward, allowing him to use his forward passing to find attackers quickly.

Anderson has also found himself higher up the pitch on occasion, with the protection of his midfield partner behind him, allowing him to showcase his attacking quality.

An interesting knock-on effect of this, and a nod to England's overarching evolution, has been the intensity England have shown as they have attacked.

"We've always played with high energy and a very aggressive style off the ball, to press high," Tuchel explained. "Now we have added another layer.

"[Now, our] intensity was very high on the ball. We did a lot of high intensity runs, a lot of counter movements, and invested a lot in counter pressing.

Anderson's ability to counter-press is an individual example of this improvement but more collective changes have contributed to England's increased intensity in possession.

In the World Cup, the system looked like a 4-3-3 on paper.

The two centre-backs and holding midfielder formed a triangle. On both flanks, a central midfielder, full-back and winger formed a triangle. Harry Kane took a roaming role.

These wide triangles were the main method of chance creation. Key to this was constant movement as England looked to make it hard for opponents to track them.

Although this often got England's winger one-against-one, teams could match England man for man in the wide areas, especially as they fatigued and off-ball runs that rid them of their markers became less common.

England's recent 3-1-3-3 shape in possession has given them an extra player at the back but appears to have also provided better attacking dynamics.

The wide centre-back has contributed to attacking play out wide. England's full-back, winger and number ten work together and are often also joined by one of the strikers or holding midfielders.

These five players have given England a numerical advantage on the flank. This has mainly been seen down England's left.

Defensively, this provides them extra players around the ball, capable of counter-pressing with more intensity to win the ball back quickly.

Offensively, this has given them an unmarked player or two that they have often found well. By overloading the left flank, England pull opponents towards one side which has also enabled them to switch it to the opposite side for team-mates in space – often two against two.

Lewis Hall has stood out in this system displaying a great chemistry with former club team-mate Anthony Gordon. Hall has taken a wide position frequently, allowing his winger to move in-field playing closer to the striker.

This winger is often the free man.

Tuchel highlighted England's 'counter-movements' as part of their improvement and the swapping and replacing of zones between Hall and Anthony Gordon have been a good example of this.

The best example, however, has probably been in the form of Kane and Gordon.

The Barcelona winger hugged the touchline for much of the World Cup, being released in behind before crossing it, rather than finding space in the box.

England's wide overloads and Hall's role have resulted in Gordon playing more central for longer parts of the game, allowing him to work more closely with Kane.

With Kane dropping deep, defenders are pulled out of position, a trigger which Gordon has used brilliantly to make runs the opposite way.

The use of runners attacking space Kane creates is not new - Jude Bellingham and Morgan Rogers have previously found joy exploiting it, but Gordon has been the latest beneficiary, while starting out wide.

Gordon's narrow runs from a wider starting position have been mirrored by Saka and Rogers on the other side too - a new string to England's attacking bow.

Trent Alexander-Arnold started against the Czech Republic, and took a wider position for large parts of the game that moved Saka almost permanently into a inside-right position.

From here, he appeared dangerous and provided goal threat while Alexander-Arnold assisted Gordon with a cross from out wide.

Despite this, the Real Madrid man was benched for Jarrell Quansah against Croatia with the pair starting together against the Czech Republic on Tuesday.

If asked to summarise Tuchel's England in one idea, runs off the ball would be a good answer. Perhaps this is why Trent Alexander-Arnold has found it difficult to find a place in Tuchel's squad.

"Trent is a unique player," Tuchel said. "He is not a runner.

"He is not someone who runs through the last line, who does overlaps [and] underlaps. [Saka and Trent] need to find a way to not be too static. On the right side, [we need] movement through the last line - to play with dynamic movement."

Against Croatia, Saka similarly found himself in central areas when Quansah held the width but played as a winger when Quansah moved centrally.

In both cases, Quansah was sure to make repeated runs beyond his winger.

Irrespective of his running, Alexander-Arnold's display on the ball across both games caught the eye. And when it comes to off-ball movement, he has shown promising signs.

For other coaches, that alone may have guaranteed him a starting spot in future but what is evident is that for Tuchel, there are underlying principles that take precedent - ideas we have seen him look to implement since his appointment.

In the past, England were accused of being a team of world-class individuals without a system.

Tuchel, more than ever, is looking to land on a world-class system.

It is up to the players to convince him of their role in it, even as it evolves.

title: Senior figures worried about Man City being in next season's Champions League
description: Senior figures within the English game are concerned that Manchester City could play in the Champions League next season even if they are relegated for breaching financial regulations.
fullText:
Senior figures within the English game are concerned that Manchester City could play in the Champions League next season even if they are relegated for breaching financial regulations.

It centres around the possibility that City win the Champions League, which would provide qualification for the competition as titleholders - regardless of their status in the English domestic pyramid.

BBC Sport has been told that there is no automatic mechanism to remove City from a European competition they qualify for on sporting merit.

An independent commission found City guilty of all charges related to inflating sponsorship revenue by £830m by using sham contracts, as well as hiding other expenses worth an additional £90m.

Without this, the independent commission said, City would have failed the profit and sustainability rules in all nine seasons between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

City continue to strenuously deny any wrongdoing, calling the outcome a "Premier League conspiracy". Last week the club lodged an appeal against the verdict.

BBC Sport has spoken to a number of senior figures with the game in recent days who are concerned about prospect of City qualifying for the Champions League next season.

The feeling is that if City do not win their appeal and are therefore handed a strong sanction, then being allowed to compete alongside Europe's elite, and receiving the financial rewards which come with it, would not be acceptable.

The immediate issue surrounds the Uefa licence, which every club needs in order to play in Europe.

One source said the issue of City's licence "had been raised" and that a solution "would require the sort of joined up thinking that's been a bit lacking so far".

The licences are issued by the Football Association, though the process itself is delegated to the Premier League.

The licences are based upon current information which does not take into account sanctions or breaches related to historical offences.

If a club fulfils all minimum criteria required for admission, the licence cannot be refused.

The key reasons a club may fail relate to overdue payables to other teams, players or outstanding tax liabilities.

Match-fixing convictions within the last 10 years, or a integrity conflict related to multi-club ownership, are considered but would not apply to City.

A source added that "licences are awarded on the basis of current financial performance, so the grounds to refuse one are unclear".

If the verdict is upheld by the appeal board is it likely City will face severe sanctions, which could include heavy points deductions, a large fine and transfer embargos.

The sanctioning hearing, which will determine the level of punishment City must face, is yet to be scheduled.

While a points deduction could rule City out of qualifying by league position, it might still be achieved through cup competitions.

Expelling City from the Premier League immediately is also an option which remains on the table.

The intricate web Man City spun to con the Premier League

Rival clubs want range of punishments for Man City

Which clubs did Man City's 'inflated' money flow to in transfer market?

Senior figures both in the English game and in European football are aware of how bad the optics would be if City face strong sanctions yet still play in the Champions League.

It is exacerbated by doubts that the whole process - including an appeal against the sanction - is not guaranteed to be completed by the end of the season.

The Premier League added new clauses to its regulations to set timeframes around disciplinary processes and appeals in the summer.

If applicable, this would mean a judgement on the sanction must come no later than January. But there is no confirmation this applies to the City case.

It is not just about City winning the Champions League, however. If they were to win the FA Cup or Carabao Cup - they play Brighton in the fourth round on 28 October - that would provide a place in the Europa League or the Conference League respectively.

European football's governing body cannot take any action while the Premier League disciplinary process plays out, but it is understood that potential scenarios are likely to be discussed by the Uefa administration and the Uefa club financial control body (CFCB).

The Premier League case found City guilty of five charges of breaching Uefa's profit and sustainability rules.

Uefa may open a case in accordance with the disciplinary regulations to find a way to remove City's eligibility.

But this does not provide certainly as City's offences are historical.

In 2020, City successfully overturned their two-year ban from European club competitions handed down by Uefa.

Uefa issued the ban after ruling City had committed "serious breaches" of financial fair play regulations between 2012 and 2016 - with the same period as the Premier League's investigation.

But the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) overturned the ban because the offences were "time-barred" under Uefa's rules.

If City are not successful in their appeal and win the Champions League, the CFCB will have to find a disciplinary measure to remove the club from next season's competition.

Yet with City already having won against Uefa through Cas once before, there is the concern they could do so again.

title: Trump looms over Susan Collins and Troy Jackson's first Maine Senate debate
description:
Susan Collins; Troy Jackson. (Getty)
Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson debated for the first time Tuesday in Maine, trading attacks over President Donald Trump, the cost of living and abortion in one of the most closely watched Senate races in the country.
Maine is central to Democrats’ path to the Senate majority as they try to capitalize on Trump’s unpopularity. Jackson tried to do just that Tuesday by tying Collins to Trump, name-checking him at least 20 times in one hour of debating on WGME-TV.
fullText:
Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson debated for the first time Tuesday in Maine, trading attacks over President Donald Trump, the cost of living and abortion in one of the most closely watched Senate races in the country.

Maine is central to Democrats’ path to the Senate majority as they try to capitalize on Trump’s unpopularity. Jackson tried to do just that Tuesday by tying Collins to Trump, name-checking him at least 20 times in one hour of debating on WGME-TV.

“It matters who you stand with,” Jackson said in his opening statement. “I don’t owe Donald Trump and the billionaires anything. I don’t fight for billionaires like she does.”

Collins, meanwhile, emphasized multiple instances when she opposed the Trump administration.

She also sought to localize the race and pitch her seniority — and her perch as chair of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee — as a boost to Maine. She touted $1.5 billion in federal funds that she has brought home to the state for 672 projects in the last five years, “from Madawaksa to Kittery, from Eastport to Rumford.”

“I’ve been able to bring home federal dollars to help ease the burden on our taxpayers,” Collins said.

Jackson set the tone for the debate early by connecting Collins to Trump and repeatedly saying she votes in alignment with him 96% of the time. Collins questioned the methodology of the study he cited.

In a moment that captured her tricky relationship with her party’s leader, Collins dodged two questions about whether she would stand with Trump if he visited Maine, with Trump having recently teased a visit to the Pine Tree State. Collins said only that she doesn’t expect him to come and that she’s “not exactly his favorite senator.”

Collins’ answer prompted a grin from Jackson. Trump has said Collins is “not my favorite person” but nevertheless endorsed her for re-election, and Vice President JD Vance has gone to Maine and backed her at events.

Polls show a neck-and-neck race between Collins and Jackson, often within the margin of error, as Collins seeks to defy gravity yet again and win a sixth term in the blue-leaning state. She is the only GOP senator representing a state Trump lost in 2024.

Both parties are spending tens of millions of dollars on a seat that carries major implications for control of the chamber, and a victory for Collins would constrict Democrats’ path to the Senate majority.

Jackson also highlighted Collins’ pivotal vote in 2018 to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who was part of the majority that overturned Roe v. Wade, doing away with the federal right to abortion. Tuesday’s debate fell on the anniversary of Kavanaugh’s confirmation vote in the Senate.

Collins said she judges all nominees by their qualifications, and she noted that she also supported justices who voted to uphold Roe v. Wade.

“In fact, I am the only Republican senator to have voted for Justice [Sonia] Sotomayor, [Elena] Kagan and [Ketanji Brown] Jackson, who were nominated by a Democratic senator,” Collins said.

Collins also hit back against attempts to tie her to the end of Roe v. Wade, referring to Jackson’s more conservative stance on abortion earlier in his career and quipping, “There’s only one of us on this stage who has always been pro-choice, and that’s me.”

Jackson did not engage with the barb in the moment, but he noted in his closing statement that he pushed for progressive abortion policies in the Legislature.

Jackson’s spokesperson, Dan Gottlieb, told NBC News earlier Tuesday that he would oppose any Trump Supreme Court nominee in his final two years should a vacancy open up — a view shared by some other Democrats.

Jackson also said Collins voted to advance Trump’s “big, beautiful bill,” which included about $1 trillion in unpopular Medicaid cuts.

That sparked a brushback from Collins, who noted that she voted against the legislation when it came to final passage. She said she has “never voted” to cut Medicaid.

“He knows I voted against President Trump’s signature legislative accomplishment,” Collins said, adding that she used the process to support a $50 billion rural healthcare fund.

“Sen. Collins is like an arsonist who helped set the fire, and she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out,” he said. “She could have stopped it.”

Collins went after Jackson’s “failed” policies as a state lawmaker, connecting them to higher housing costs and property taxes. She also questioned his talents as a legislator and whether he could be effective as a junior senator in a divided Senate.

When the topic turned to immigration, Jackson cited an ICE officer’s killing of a Mainer this year, saying it happened because “Sen. Collins would not push back against ICE.”

Collins said the shooting was “horrific” and “demonstrates that ICE needs further reform.” She said that she supported increased funding for body-worn cameras, as well as training of officers, and that she teamed up with the Maine delegation to demand answers from the Trump administration.

In her closing statement, Collins said: “To be effective in the Senate, you need knowledge, experience, seniority and relationships. That combination has allowed me to pass bipartisan legislation.”

Jackson questioned whether she has used her power well.

“Tonight, Sen. Collins has told us how powerful she is,” he said in his closing statement. “But power means nothing if you won’t use it when the people may need it.”

title: Army sets date for Fort Hood mass shooter Nidal Hasan to face firing squad
description:
Nidal Hasan, who was sentenced to death for the 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, will be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3, according to a memo from the acting Army secretary.
The execution, the first carried out by the U.S. military in more than 60 years, is scheduled for 1 p.
fullText:
It will be the first U.S. military execution in more than 60 years.

Nidal Hasan, who was sentenced to death for the 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, will be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3, according to a memo from the acting Army secretary.

The execution, the first carried out by the U.S. military in more than 60 years, is scheduled for 1 p.m. CT, according to the memo issued Tuesday by acting Army Secretary Adam Telle.

The Pentagon announced Monday that Hasan would be executed by firing squad after President Donald Trump approved the decision Friday.

Under the military’s execution process for prisoners on death row, the Army secretary initiates the proceedings, which then require approval from the defense secretary and eventually the president.

Under Army policy, executions must happen within 150 days of the president approving it, but no sooner than 60 days.

The military has not executed a service member since 1961, when Pvt. John Bennett was put to death after being convicted of the rape and attempted murder of an 11-year-old girl in Austria.

On Nov. 5, 2009, Hasan, then an Army psychiatrist, opened fire at the Soldier Readiness Processing Center at the Fort Hood military base, killing 12 soldiers and one civilian before he was shot, severely wounded and arrested.

Hasan was convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted murder and sentenced to death in 2013. He was sent to a military detention center at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas.

He is one of four death row inmates in the Army justice system.

The announcement of his execution comes after ABC News reported in June that the Army had been planning military executions, according to internal documents and officials familiar with the matter.

Army regulation dictates that at least two media outlets should be selected to witness the execution.

title: Bessent says inflation and bond yields will drop after the Iran war. Others aren't so sure.
description:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says the economy is "accelerating" and inflation, along with bond yields, will come back down once the conflict in Iran ends. 
"Right now, we have this energy shock that's generated by the Iran conflict, and headline inflation is about 3.5%. But my message is underlying inflation — core inflation — is down to about 2.3%," Bessent said at the Pennsylvania Chamber of Commerce on Monday night.
fullText:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says the economy is "accelerating" and inflation, along with bond yields, will come back down once the conflict in Iran ends.

"Right now, we have this energy shock that's generated by the Iran conflict, and headline inflation is about 3.5%. But my message is underlying inflation — core inflation — is down to about 2.3%," Bessent said at the Pennsylvania Chamber of Commerce on Monday night.

He asserted that median wage growth is in line with headline inflation, and that "we will get to the other side of this Iran conflict. Energy will come back down, and the wage growth will continue."

He said 1 million private sector jobs have been created this year, while government jobs have been trimmed by 300,000.

"Real wage growth comes from private sector jobs, and I think we're just starting to see the acceleration here," he said.

But not everyone sees the wage picture the same.

Gregory Daco, chief economist for EY, notes that average hourly earnings rose at an annualized pace of 3% in September, marking the slowest pace of the post-pandemic cycle. He said he expects inflation in September, as measured by the Consumer Price Index, to clock in at 3.6%, and as a result, he anticipates that wages adjusted for inflation will likely fall 0.6% year over year, marking a sixth consecutive month of contraction.

"While strong wealth effects from stock market gains continue to support solid aggregate consumer spending, the growing income squeeze affecting households is likely to cap spending growth heading into 2027," Daco said.

Joe Brusuelas, chief economist for RSM, agrees that the economy accelerated into the third quarter, but he asserts that inflation is not easing, pressuring wages and purchasing power.

Brusuelas maintains that the CPI report due out next week will show that wage growth adjusted for inflation has been flat to negative since the start of the Iran war.

"It's far more likely that declining real wages begin to act as a mild drag on growth heading into the final quarter of 2026 and early 2027," he said.

Bessent also addressed the spike in long-term Treasury yields, saying he believes the run-up is a function of headline inflation and higher energy prices stemming from the war. Once the conflict ends, he said, longer-term bond yields will come down to levels seen in mid-February before the war.

"I don't know if this conflict's going to end next week, next month, in two months, but I believe on the other side of this, energy prices will be much lower and interest rates, mortgage rates will come back down," he said.

title: How a protest over missing teachers spread to 1,800 schools across France
description:
Students chant slogans during a demonstration against under-resourced schools, in Paris, Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026.
                                                                                    |
                                                                                                                                                        Teresa...
fullText:
What began as protests over missing teachers, overcrowded classrooms and deteriorating schools has grown into a nationwide crisis in France, drawing hundreds of thousands into the streets and triggering violent clashes between demonstrators and police.

Students say years of underinvestment have left them with teacher shortages, long school days and deteriorating facilities. The government says those legitimate concerns have been overtaken by violent groups, while unions and opposition parties accuse officials of responding to young protesters with excessive force.

The Union Syndicale Lyceenne, a high school students’ union, said the movement had reached a “new record” on Tuesday, claiming 1,800 schools were blocked, disrupted or closed. Less than three weeks earlier, it had all begun at a single school outside Paris.

On Sept. 17, teachers at Lycee Antoine-de-Saint-Exupery, a high school in a suburb southeast of Paris, went on strike over unfilled positions, including those of a math teacher, French teacher, history teacher, school nurse and social worker.

Students joined the teachers the next day and blockaded the school on Monday, Sept. 21. Lawmakers from France’s hard-left party, La France Insoumise (LFI), were present at the blockade, sparking debate over whether the party helped fuel the protests ahead of April’s presidential election.

Laurent Bessiere, a math teacher at the school, is among those who remain skeptical of the party’s involvement.

“We can’t help but think that perhaps some people want to exploit the situation, but we certainly didn’t get involved in that,” Bessiere told France Inter.

The day of the blockade, students marched to the regional education office, where staffing decisions for their school are made, and requested a meeting to demand that the vacant positions be filled.

The students were granted a meeting a few days later and were surprised by how successful the protest had been.

“We were quite proud of ourselves because we didn’t think the blockade would go this far,” Tessa, a student at Saint-Exupery, told France Inter. “Even though some people were just doing it to skip classes, we managed to get answers to our problems and even some solutions.”

Although the students were granted a meeting and the school received a new director of vocational and technological training, tensions continued to rise. Firework mortars were set off inside the school on Sept. 23, and classes were canceled the next day after a bomb threat.

Another high school north of Paris set up its own blockade on Sept. 25. Within a week, the movement had reached more than 1,000 schools.

Although missing teachers were the original spark, with students describing waiting weeks or longer for substitutes, the movement has expanded beyond staffing to address the broader conditions students face in public schools.

On social media platforms such as TikTok and Instagram, students have described rundown classrooms with more than 30 students. They are demanding smaller class sizes and shorter school days.

According to EUalive, students’ placards at a protest at Lamartine high school read, “8 a.m. to 6 p.m. More hours of lessons than sleep.” Manon Aubry, an LFI member of the European Parliament, quoted a student as saying, “We can’t study surrounded by cockroaches and windows falling on us.”

The movement is also addressing inequalities between schools in poorer suburbs and those in wealthier areas. Some students from wealthier parts of Paris say they have joined the protests because they recognize the gap between conditions at their schools and those in poorer areas, where students have expressed concerns about their futures.

“They say we can’t become engineers, doctors, when every person here can succeed,” Human, a senior at the school where the protests originated, told France Inter.

Although students are united on their demands, they disagree over tactics, with many rejecting the violence and feeling uneasy about the direction the protests have taken.

A student at the origin school told France Inter she’s troubled by schools where students are “having fun damaging, burning trash cans,” and a junior in Lorraine told L’Est Republicain that “It’s not right, even if the demands are legitimate. There’s no point in burning down the high school, even if it is the only way to make yourselves heard.”

As the movement spread beyond the school where it began, its lack of central leadership made it increasingly difficult to control. Students with different motives joined the demonstrations, along with people who did not attend the schools involved.

Some participants set off fireworks, damaged property and threw objects at police, leading government officials to argue that what began as a legitimate student movement had been overtaken by people seeking confrontation.

Thursday marked a shift in what security forces described as more radical rhetoric. Arson destroyed the entrance hall of Nelson-Mandela high school in Nantes, and a firetruck was looted and burned in Marseille.

Some students have blamed outsiders for the increasing acts of violence. A student at Nelson-Mandela told France 3 Pays de la Loire that the violence “was caused by people from outside our school, and we don’t know anything about their demands.”

The government responded by deploying riot police to schools and demonstrations across the country. Officers have used tear gas and dispersal grenades to break up crowds, while thousands of protesters, most of whom are minors, have been arrested.

The tactics have drawn scrutiny after several teenagers were seriously injured, including a 15-year-old who lost his hand after reportedly picking up a police grenade during a clash in northern France. Conflicting accounts regarding the incident have made it one of 10 investigations being conducted by the General Inspectorate of the National Police.

On Tuesday, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu told the National Assembly that 215 students, 85 school workers, and 715 police officers had been injured since the protests began, with arrests at about 6,100.

French officials have said that the students’ original concerns about teacher shortages and school conditions are legitimate. Lecornu has directed government ministers to consider how quickly absent teachers can be replaced, whether the length of the school day should be reviewed and what repairs are needed in aging school buildings, with initial proposals expected by the end of October.

At the same time, the government argues that the movement has changed as it has spread. Officials have described the escalating clashes as “urban violence” and accused LFI and other far-left groups of exploiting students’ concerns for political purposes. The government has defended deploying riot police as necessary to protect schools and restore order, even as students, teachers and opposition leaders criticize its response as disproportionate.

“Many false reports have circulated about the actions of law enforcement,” Lecornu posted on X. “Instructions on proportionality have been given to police officers and gendarmes. What triggers their intervention is violence … the situation is serious enough without needing a political class that fans the flames and stokes the violence.”

Depuis plusieurs jours, l’ultra-violence a frappé à la porte de nos lycées. Des élèves, des personnels éducatifs, des policiers et des gendarmes ont été blessés. Ces violences doivent être condamnées sans condition.

Beaucoup de fausses informations ont circulé sur l’action des…

LFI has openly supported the student movement while denying the government’s claims that it organized or fueled the unrest.

Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of LFI, called the government’s crackdown irresponsible and has accused Lecornu of ordering repression against the students.

“This ferocity is irresponsible with an obvious racist aftertaste,” Melenchon posted. “Hands off our youth. Elected officials and activists, step in wherever you can.”

Les lycéens en mouvement sont inoffensifs. Le gouvernement Lecornu a ordonné la répression. Cette férocité est irresponsable avec un arrière-goût raciste évident. Pas touche à nos jeunes. Élus et militants insoumis interposez-vous partout où vous le pouvez.

Marine Le Pen and the far-right National Rally have focused primarily on security, portraying the unrest as evidence that the government has lost control. Le Pen has promised to restore safety in French schools and called for a new law making participation in a riot a clearly defined offense.

“The Republic must guarantee the right to demonstrate,” Le Pen posted on X. “But it also must recall a simple boundary: no cause justifies violence.”

La République doit garantir le droit de manifester. Mais elle doit aussi rappeler une frontière simple : aucune cause ne justifie la violence.

Lorsque la violence devient une méthode politique, c’est toujours la liberté de chacun d’entre vous qui est menacée. pic.twitter.com/MubWPi0ri7

The protests come about six months before France’s presidential election, and give each party an opportunity to reinforce its message. LFI is presenting itself as an ally of frustrated students, while the National Rally is emphasizing law and order, and President Emmanuel Macron’s allies are trying to show they can address students’ concerns while maintaining control.

French authorities estimated that more than 250,000 people demonstrated across the country Tuesday, while organizers placed turnout at 450,000. Although some demonstrations were peaceful, clashes broke out in several cities, police used tear gas and water cannons, and nearly 500 people were arrested.

The government is now opening a national student consultation and directing high schools to hold forums where students can discuss their concerns. Ministers are expected to present their first proposals by the end of October, but no agreement has been reached, and it remains to be seen whether those steps will be enough to end the blockades and demonstrations across the country.

title: U.S. pushes Russia for information on suspected plague death
description:
Health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor says no special measures have been ordered regarding a reported plague death in Russia (Igor IVANKO)
The United States made a formal request pressing Russia for information on the reported plague death of a laboratory technician, a source close to the matter said Tuesday, as calls grew for transparency from Moscow.
Russian authorities have denied that they are imposing anti-plague measures and played down the reports of an incident at a plague research institute in Siberia's Irkutsk region last week.
But US President Donald Trump said he would speak soon with Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the World Health Organization's head called on Moscow to be open about the situation. 
"We have officially requested additional information from the Russian government," a State Department spokesperson said Tuesday.
"We are also in official communication with other countries around the world to share information," they added.
fullText:
The United States made a formal request pressing Russia for information on the reported plague death of a laboratory technician, a source close to the matter said Tuesday, as calls grew for transparency from Moscow.

Russian authorities have denied that they are imposing anti-plague measures and played down the reports of an incident at a plague research institute in Siberia's Irkutsk region last week.

But US President Donald Trump said he would speak soon with Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the World Health Organization's head called on Moscow to be open about the situation.

"We have officially requested additional information from the Russian government," a State Department spokesperson said Tuesday.

"We are also in official communication with other countries around the world to share information," they added.

The request for information was sent via a confidential diplomatic communication, known as a demarche, according to a source close to the matter.

During a trip to Iceland, Rubio said: "We encourage Russia to be transparent and share more information with the world so that all of us could react accordingly and appropriately."

Trump later said he would be speaking to Putin about what happened.

"I have a call scheduled, yes," Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he had spoken to Putin, adding that it would happen "very soon."

Asked what US intelligence agencies were saying about the situation, Trump said: "We're in very deep discussions. We'll be able to report on it probably tomorrow."

- Cause of death 'undetermined' -

Russian news outlet People of Baikal reported Friday that the dead woman -- named as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova -- may have contracted pneumonic plague from a broken test tube.

Other media reported a possible link between her death and a lab accident at the facility.

The People of Baikal outlet also said up to 200 people with whom she may have had contact were under quarantine.

But Russian authorities say the cause of death is not confirmed and health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor has denied claims circulating in a document online that special measures had been put in place.

"We wish to clarify that the document and information in question do not originate from official sources and are untrue," it said on Telegram.

Russian officials said postmortem tests had not detected the disease.

Irkutsk Regional Governor Igor Kobzev said Monday that an inspection by health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor had found the woman died of pneumonia and the cause was "undetermined."

"No microorganisms linked to the young woman's professional work were found in her biological samples," he said, adding that no other staff at the institute had sought medical attention since her death.

WHO said that an update received Tuesday from Russia stressed that "no case of this dangerous disease has been recorded in the city of Irkutsk."

But its director Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus later urged Moscow to be transparent, saying WHO had "requested further information" on the cause of the pneumonia case and other details.

"Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks," he wrote on X.

Plague is a bacterial disease that can occur in several forms, including pneumonic plague, which is the most contagious type and can be transmitted by respiratory means. Bubonic plague is transmitted by infected fleas.

Pneumonic plague, which causes lung failure, can be fatal if not treated early, according to WHO.

Trump said Monday he was ready to help Russia if needed.

But in an apparent response to Trump's offer, the Russian watchdog said Tuesday that Moscow was prepared to assist the US in combating its own outbreaks of infectious diseases.

It highlighted a "significantly worsened" measles situation in three US states, and a "fatal case of plague" recorded in New Mexico in June, among other things.

Measles cases have increased under the Trump administration, in which vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr serves as health secretary.

An international conference on plague and other infectious diseases will be held in Irkutsk on October 21-22, although organizers said it was "unrelated to the recent death of an employee of the anti-plague institute."
