title: Russia stonewalls U.S. as Trump administration weighs risks from mysterious lab death
description:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks during a press conference at the House of Collections in Reykjavik, Iceland, on October 6, 2026. - Mark Schiefelbein/Pool/AFP/Getty Images
The Trump administration is struggling to get clear answers about the death of a Russian laboratory worker at an institute dedicated to studying the plague, amid days of stonewalling from Russian officials about the mysterious circumstances surrounding the episode.
The death of the technician at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia immediately raised alarms throughout the administration, prompting a race to compile intel and plot for a potential public health response, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter.
But Russia’s reluctance to share information about the incident has complicated those efforts, leaving officials uncertain what broader risks it could pose — and how exactly to defend the US against them.
The US is considering issuing a formal diplomatic communication, called a démarche, to Russia for more information, a source familiar told CNN.
fullText:
The Trump administration is struggling to get clear answers about the death of a Russian laboratory worker at an institute dedicated to studying the plague, amid days of stonewalling from Russian officials about the mysterious circumstances surrounding the episode.

The death of the technician at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia immediately raised alarms throughout the administration, prompting a race to compile intel and plot for a potential public health response, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter.

But Russia’s reluctance to share information about the incident has complicated those efforts, leaving officials uncertain what broader risks it could pose — and how exactly to defend the US against them.

The US is considering issuing a formal diplomatic communication, called a démarche, to Russia 

“It’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday. “Maybe it’s bigger than we thought. We don’t know, but I think it would be reckless at this moment, given the limited information we still have, to speculate.”

US officials were in touch with the Russian government as early as last Friday, a State Department official said, including contact between the department’s health experts and the Russian Foreign Ministry. And that outreach has continued, an administration official said, as Rubio expressed hope Tuesday that the limited information sharing “will change in the next few hours and days.”

President Donald Trump told reporters outside the White House Tuesday afternoon that he had “call scheduled” to speak with Russian leader Vladimir Putin about the issue “very soon.” He added US agencies would have more information to report “probably tomorrow.”

But the US has gotten limited cooperation so far. What little information has come out of Russia has faced deep skepticism, with officials unconvinced that the Kremlin is being fully forthcoming, according to people familiar with the situation.

Still, until the administration knows more through intelligence collection and diplomatic outreach, officials are not taking steps such as putting travel restrictions into place to prevent any potential spread, according to a US official. The US already advises against travel to Russia due to various factors, including the possibility of wrongful detention and the war with Ukraine.

Among the critical questions still outstanding: whether the 28-year-old lab worker who died last week contracted pneumonic plague — a severe but treatable infection — or another, unknown infectious disease. Staff at the Anti-Plague Institute study a range of other dangerous diseases, including cholera, anthrax and brucellosis, according to the institute’s website.

US officials have also sought details on whether the disease was modified in any way, a process called gain of function that could dramatically alter the way the US and other countries might respond.

Rubio and other Trump officials have publicly downplayed the immediate threat to Americans, emphasizing that the administration is closely monitoring the situation and that pneumonic plague is treatable with antibiotics.

But behind the scenes, there is deep unease within the administration over the continued lack of insight, the people familiar with the situation said. Compounding those concerns is the Russian government’s outsized response, including quarantining the hospital where the lab worker was treated, according to the mayor of the Shelekhovsky district. Nearly 200 people are under observation, a regional news outlet reported.

“We don’t know a lot right now about what actually happened,” said one US official. “But one thing most of us feel certain about: The Russians are going to act like the Chinese did with Covid. They won’t be forthcoming.”

Still, Trump on Monday characterized the situation as a “big problem” for Russia, suggesting that the US might need to provide some unspecified level of aid.

In a statement, a State Department spokesperson said that several federal agencies were “closely monitoring the fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague,” but that many of the details surrounding it remained unconfirmed. They reiterated that Americans have long been advised not to travel to Russia for any reason.

“We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly,” the spokesperson said.

In the days since the lab worker’s death, the National Security Council and State Department officials have led the administration’s push to gather information, piece together what happened and evaluate the potential risks, officials and others familiar with the situation said. Federal health agencies, including the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response, have also been involved in the cross-government effort.

A source familiar with the outreach said Trump officials have also backchanneled with the World Health Organization — the international health body that Trump pulled funding from soon after taking office, but that the government has continued to communicate with in emergency situations.

WHO said Monday that it was in contact with Russian authorities to verify details about the lab worker’s death, though it has so far also received little information.

“If they’re not transparent, if they’re not open to independent accountability, how is it possible to trust the Kremlin is telling us the full and accurate information?” said Lawrence Gostin, a global health law professor at Georgetown University who has worked closely with WHO. “Clearly, on its face, the lab was conducting extremely high-risk research and using shoddy biosafety measures.”

The Anti-Plague Institute’s relatively remote location in eastern Russia, combined with the pneumonic plague’s limited ability to quickly spread, has given health experts some comfort that any immediate threat can be contained.

Pneumonic plague is a bacterial infection, unlike the highly transmissible coronavirus strain that sparked the 2020 pandemic. And while the plague is fatal if untreated, there are now effective and widely available antibiotics to treat it.

While there is little indication that the incident will touch off another global health crisis, officials and outside experts said it has nevertheless reinforced how difficult it can be to monitor and prepare for potential biological threats.

The Health and Human Services Department may have the medical stockpile necessary to combat conventional pneumonic plague, those officials and experts said. But there’s little certainty whether it could do the same against a modified version — or how long it would take to develop a treatment if needed.

Jennifer Nuzzo, an epidemiology professor and director of the Pandemic Center at Brown University School of Public Health, said the episode also comes as health response capabilities both in the US and globally have been diminished by funding cuts and the strain of responding to other crises. WHO has proposed slashing its budget following a $600 million shortfall triggered by the US’ exit.

America’s ability to handle a new public health response, meanwhile, “is severely diminished” amid its efforts to combat measles outbreaks, she said.

“We are talking about a very depleted system. God forbid you layer another pathogen onto the already laborious and difficult work of going after measles,” said Nuzzo. “That would be a nightmare.”

This story has been updated with additional details.

title: Will Trump's executive order on dyed diesel lower prices? Experts explain.
description:
President Donald Trump has issued an executive order that makes a specific kind of tax-exempt diesel fuel reserved for farm and construction equipment available to a broad set of road vehicles in an effort to reduce overall diesel costs.
The type of diesel, known as dyed diesel, is exempt from a 24.4-cent per gallon federal tax, making it a lower-priced option than regular diesel. Some states expanded access to dyed diesel in a similar fashion over recent weeks, providing relief from state diesel taxes.
Dyed diesel is nearly identical to regular diesel, besides a small amount of dye used by law enforcement officers and inspectors to ensure only permitted vehicle owners avail themselves of the fuel.
fullText:
The move aimed to lower costs for farmers weeks before the midterm elections.

President Donald Trump has issued an executive order that makes a specific kind of tax-exempt diesel fuel reserved for farm and construction equipment available to a broad set of road vehicles in an effort to reduce overall diesel costs.

The type of diesel, known as dyed diesel, is exempt from a 24.4-cent per gallon federal tax, making it a lower-priced option than regular diesel. Some states expanded access to dyed diesel in a similar fashion over recent weeks, providing relief from state diesel taxes.

Dyed diesel is nearly identical to regular diesel, besides a small amount of dye used by law enforcement officers and inspectors to ensure only permitted vehicle owners avail themselves of the fuel.

The executive order on Monday came weeks ahead of the midterm elections, targeting costs associated with a fuel vital to the supply chain for everything from groceries to clothing to electronics.

The White House called on federal agencies to defer payment of federal road taxes over the remainder of 2026, and seek out ways to relieve payment of the deferred taxes.

"Farmers and truckers are essential to the American way of life. Restricted global diesel supply has led to rising prices, and these key industries have been particularly hard hit," the White House said in its executive order.

"While my Administration has already undertaken historic efforts to ensure fuel affordability for our citizens, it is clear that further temporary relief is necessary," the White House added.

In theory, a meaningful reduction in diesel prices could lower expenses for farmers and truckers, while easing the cost burden for shoppers crunched by a rise of inflation.

A host of factors will complicate the effectiveness of the order, however, some analysts told ABC News. Dyed diesel is sold at a limited set of locations designed primarily for industry operators, constraining access to the fuel.

Expansion of vehicles eligible for dyed diesel, meanwhile, could prompt a surge in demand for the fuel, exceeding available supply and putting upward pressure on prices at the pump, some analysts said.

"On paper and in the press, it sounds like it might be significant, especially ahead of the midterms. However, like many things, the paper doesn’t always match the intended reality," Patrick De Haan, a petroleum analyst at GasBuddy, said in a post on Substack.

All in all, analysts who spoke to ABC News downplayed the potential impact of Trump's decree, saying savings would be modest for farmers, who already enjoy access to dyed diesel for their energy-intensive agricultural equipment.

The move could shed nearly 25 cents per gallon from the cost of diesel for vehicle owners newly allowed to access the tax-exempt fuel, but those savings make up a small share of the price increase for diesel set off by the Iran war, analysts said.

The average price of a gallon of diesel stands at $6.31, marking an increase of $2.63, or about 70%, from a year earlier, AAA data shows.

A truck with a 150-gallon tank, for example, runs its owner about $948 for a fill-up at current diesel prices. A deduction of 24.4 cents per gallon would remove $36 from that bill.

"This is a way to try to use executive power to try to provide short-term relief," said Timothy Fitzgerald, a University of Tennessee professor of business economics who studies the petroleum industry. "But you’ve seen a very large increase in retail prices. The tax relief will help but it won’t offset the underlying difference in prices."

Meanwhile, the savings will likely be muted or nonexistent for products on store shelves, analysts added, since diesel prices make up a fraction of the costs that feed into the price of any given product.

Every dollar spent on food, for instance, usually includes three or four cents that stem from transportation costs, Omair Sharif, founder of Inflation Insights, previously told ABC News.

David Ortega, a food economist at Michigan State University, said he expects any potential price relief on grocery store shelves to be "negligible."

"If you look at how the price of fuel factors into overall food costs, we’re talking about a single-digit [percentage] share of overall food costs. This is not something that will really be driving prices down meaningfully," Ortega added.

Tom Seng, a professor of energy finance at Texas Christian University, echoed the view. "I don’t think this will be significant enough that we’ll see food prices in general come down," Seng told ABC News.

To be sure, the price savings for eligible diesel buyers could prove more significant in states that offered up an exemption from state-level taxes, compounding the benefit of the federal tax exemption.

A handful of states have granted their own waiver for dyed diesel, including important midterm states like Nebraska, North Carolina and Texas, De Haan said. Georgia and Ohio recently suspended their diesel taxes, offering their own version of relief.

The state-by-state policy differences could pose a challenge for interstate truckers, however, deterring some vehicle owners who fear local law enforcement, De Haan said.

Various impediments will limit the effect of the executive order, Ortega said. "It’s not really going to make a whole lot of difference," he added.

title: Trump doesn't commit to repaying $12 million in federal funds spent on controversial ads
description:
— A day after President Donald Trump said he would start paying for controversial taxpayer-funded ads with a campaign account, there's no sign he plans to refund the millions of federal dollars already spent on them.
Nearly $12 million worth of ads have already aired, according to AdImpact, as part of the $20 million the Department of Homeland Security tapped for the contract.
But Trump's plan to pay for the ads with MAGA Inc. doesn't mean there's any reimbursement coming, said a White House official who was not authorized to talk publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
Speaking to reporters Tuesday, Trump said the ads were "really good" and "promotion for the country, done by many presidents before.
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A day after President Donald Trump said he would start paying for controversial taxpayer-funded ads with a campaign account, there's no sign he plans to refund the millions of federal dollars already spent on them.

Nearly $12 million worth of ads have already aired, according to AdImpact, as part of the $20 million the Department of Homeland Security tapped for the contract.

But Trump's plan to pay for the ads with MAGA Inc. doesn't mean there's any reimbursement coming, said a White House official who was not authorized to talk publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.

Speaking to reporters Tuesday, Trump said the ads were "really good" and "promotion for the country, done by many presidents before." Asked whether he'd repay the funds already spent, he said, "We'll decide."

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer slammed Trump for not committing to reimbursement and said he believes the president's plan for covering future costs represents illegal coordination with his super PAC.

"Trump must return this money to the American people and there must be a full investigation into this gross waste and abuse of taxpayer dollars," Schumer told The Associated Press.

The ads, which began airing in late September, glorify Trump and echo his political messaging going into the midterms. One features a clip of Trump talking about the threat of communism and another is a replay of an ad from his last presidential campaign. The fifth ad in the campaign began airing Tuesday, focusing on the Trump administration's capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro.

Republicans and Democrats alike have said the ads aren't an appropriate use of U.S. government money. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a Republican from South Dakota, said they shouldn't be paid for with taxpayer dollars.

The Trump administration tapped $20 million from the Department of Homeland Security to pay for the campaign-style ads glorifying the president that have drawn widespread criticism. Two top Democratic senators said last week that the money is being drawn from Trump's so-called "One Big Beautiful Bill" and was supposed to go toward U.S. Customs and Border Protection.

Republican Sen. Katie Britt of Alabama, who chairs the panel that oversees DHS funding, said Tuesday that she had not yet seen Trump's ads, but she said taxpayer money should be used as intended.

"We'll take a look at that," Britt said at the Capitol. "You want to make sure that any use of taxpayer dollars is done judiciously and in accordance with the law."

Legal experts said the ads might even violate federal statutes, including a law against congressionally appropriated money being used for "publicity or propaganda" and another limiting the partisan political activities of government employees.

The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements similar to what past administrations have done to promote policies. Trump on Monday posted on his Truth Social platform calling the ads "positive promotion for our Great U.S.A." while also promising to pay for them with "money I raised for MAGA Inc."

That is Trump's political war chest, which had amassed more than $400 million by the end of July. Trump has begun tapping it to boost Republican candidates across the country in the midterm elections.

AP Congressional Correspondent Lisa Mascaro contributed to this report.

title: Washington resident accused of helping plan Canada's Tumbler Ridge school shooting
description:
People pay their respects at a memorial on the steps of the Town Hall, following a vigil the previous day, in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, Canada, Feb. 14, 2026. - Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press/AP
US authorities have announced the arrest of a 30-year-old from Washington state in connection with the February school shooting in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia.
The person, identified by authorities as James Cody Bryant, was arrested in Bellingham, Washington, on Tuesday morning on a charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country, according to an announcement by the US Justice Department. The February attack on a secondary school in the small town of Tumbler Ridge was Canada’s deadliest school shooting in decades, leaving eight people dead, including six children, and dozens wounded.
fullText:
US authorities have arrested a 30-year-old from Washington state in connection with the February school shooting in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia.

James Cody Bryant was arrested in Bellingham, Washington, on Tuesday morning on a charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country, according to the US Justice Department. The February attack on a secondary school in the small town at the foothills of the Rocky Mountains was Canada’s deadliest school shooting in decades, leaving eight people dead, including six children, and dozens wounded.

Bryant appeared in court Tuesday afternoon in Seattle. CNN has reached out to Bryant’s lawyer for comment. A hearing has been set for October 20.

Bryant was allegedly “in repeated contact with” the 18-year-old Canadian shooter, Jesse Van Rootselaar, “offering advice, sending money and even agreeing to live stream the horrific event” on Twitch, said Neil Floyd, the acting US attorney for the Western District of Washington, at a press conference in Seattle.

The money Bryant gave the shooter amounted to a little over $100, primarily to buy a lighter and a pair of shoes that Van Rootselaar “wanted to have when she conducted this killing spree,” Floyd said. The two discussed sending weapons to Van Rootselaar, but Bryant was uncomfortable with doing so and refused, according to a complaint filed in court on Friday.

Bryant began an online friendship with Van Rootselaar after meeting on video chatting website Omegle three years before the shooting, authorities said. An affidavit within the complaint includes excerpts of chat logs between Bryant and Van Rootselaar on the Discord website.

“I read a lot of court documents, including some that discuss incredibly heinous acts of violence, but this complaint was particularly difficult to read,” said FBI agent Mike Harrington at the Tuesday press conference, “in part because of the casual tone these two individuals used when discussing the mass taking of innocent lives that was being planned.”

In one exchange, Van Rootselaar allegedly told Bryant that she wanted to “avoid doing a school” but that “there’s just so many reasons why it’s ideal.” According to the affidavit, Bryant responded in turn that attacking a hotel “seems like a good idea.”

After Van Rootselaar killed two family members, Bryant allegedly offered the attacker advice on how to fix a car when it failed to start en route to the school.

Canadian and US authorities have said that Bryant and Van Rootselaar, who died in the shooting, are trans women, though officials used male and female pronouns interchangeably to describe the two throughout the press conference.

Assistant Commissioner Elija Rain of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police said Canadian authorities contacted the US Department of Homeland Security soon after the shooting, based on “information from one of the online platforms used by the shooter.”

“As further alleged, instead of de-escalating or reporting to law enforcement, Bryant continued to enable the shooter over the months they discussed these plans,” said Harrington. “In addition to providing money, technical advice and particular items to be used in the shooting, Bryant agreed to record a live stream feed of the attack and broadcast it in a way that would maximize notoriety for the shooter.”

It was not previously known that anyone apart from Van Rootselaar allegedly participated in planning the massacre. CNN previously reported Van Rootselaar posted about guns and hunting and her apparent mental health struggles online in the lead up to the massacre.

Seven families of victims sued tech company OpenAI in April after information emerged that the shooter had used ChatGPT to plan the attack. The week before the suit was filed, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman apologized to the community for not alerting law enforcement after Van Rootselaar’s account was banned.

CNN’s Josh Campbell, Paula Newton and Lex Harvey contributed reporting. This story has been updated with additional developments.

title: Delta Air Lines jet clips an Air Canada plane on LAX tarmac

title: The Picture of Dennis Hastert
description: Chris...
fullText:
The disgraced former congressman was a better representative of the GOP than the party would like to admit.

The obituaries for former Republican House speaker Dennis Hastert, who died over the weekend, all led with the scandal that justly stained his name at the end of his career—charges of child sexual abuse dating from his tenure as a teacher and wrestling coach in Yorkville, Illinois, in the 1960s and ’70s. After his subsequent resignation, Hastert was convicted on charges of bank fraud stemming from efforts to conceal a series of hush-money payments to one of his former victims; in 2016, he was sentenced to a 15-month prison term, but was released on medical grounds several weeks before serving it out.

Shortly after Hastert pleaded guilty to the fraud charges, then–Republican Speaker Paul Ryan had his official portrait removed from the Capitol, signaling the GOP’s determination to treat the disgraced party leader as a bad apple—an unfortunate behavioral outlier—best forgotten.

But Hastert’s horrifying predatory past wasn’t his only baleful contribution to our political scene. As a rising GOP power broker, Hastert followed the scorched-earth model of politics practiced by his mentor, former majority leader Tom DeLay. DeLay became majority whip in 1994, and set about transforming the GOP conference into a machine running on ideological orthodoxy and corrupt infusions of cash. His signature innovation was an initiative called the “K Street Project”—a bid to transform the DC lobbying industry into a subsidiary of the Republican Party, demanding that favored firms heighten their PAC contributions to the GOP while stiffing the Democratic opposition. DeLay, who graduated to majority leader in 2003, became a casualty of his own corruptionist political vision; in 2005, a Travis County grand jury indicted him on charges of money laundering, and he resigned from office a year later. He was also a close confrere of superlobbyist Jack Abramoff, also later jailed on fraud and corruption charges, taking the K Street Project’s amoral precepts to their logical extreme.

Hastert served as DeLay’s deputy whip, and he thrived by following DeLay’s cutthroat example. He assumed the speakership in 1999 in the rushed procedural aftermath of still another House speaker sexual scandal involving Robert Livingston, a protégé of Newt Gingrich. Once the Republicans secured new majorities in the 2002 midterms, Hastert made a point of looking out for his scandal-plagued mentor. By 2004, DeLay’s moneyed antics had become so blatant that they ran afoul of the House Committee on Standards of Official Conduct (known today as the House Ethics Committee); it convened a separate subcommittee that endorsed a series of reprimands for the majority leader. Hastert moved with swift dispatch to fire the committee chair, as well as the two GOP members of the bipartisan panel, replacing them with hack loyalists. When three DeLay cronies were indicted in Texas, Hastert got the committee to approve a rule to permit DeLay to continue serving as majority leader after he was indicted.

Hastert also followed DeLay’s example by using the power of his office to engage in corrupt self-dealing. While he served as speaker, he pulled together a series of real estate deals in his home state of Illinois that saw his net worth skyrocket into the millions; during one bitter fight over a long-stalled transportation bill, Hastert saw to it that an earmark created a new highway interchange—unwanted by both local residents and the Transportation Department—a mile away from his land parcels, causing them to escalate still further in speculative value.

Hastert’s most enduring legislative legacy, however, is the notorious “Hastert rule”—the diktat that no legislation would proceed to a floor vote unless it already won the support of the House GOP conference. This might seem like the wonky, technocratic innovation of a former deputy whip, but in reality, it cemented the 21st-century GOP’s reputation for enforcing ideological orthodoxy at all costs—at the direct expense of the negotiations, compromises, and legislative conferencing that made up what House leaders had dubbed, in a show of optimism, “regular order.” As longtime congressional scholar Norm Ornstein writes, “no speaker has done more to relegate regular order to the sidelines than Hastert.”

In combination with the DeLay mantra of using the legislative process to maximize the flow of baksheesh, Haster’s siege on regular order produced some of the ugliest spectacles seen on the contemporary House floor—most notoriously, the vote that Hastert kept open on the Bush administration’s Medicare prescription drug plan. A scheduled 15-minute canvassing swelled into three hours in the dead of night, as Hastert and his lieutenants bribed and bullied the GOP conference into submission. As Ornstein notes, this was to become the de facto business model for Congress:

Under Hastert, amendments from Democrats and Republicans alike were squelched by a strikingly pliant Rules Committee; conferences were rarely held, and if they were, it was late at night and they were closed to input from all except loyal lieutenants; and provisions were sometimes added to conference reports that had never been in either House or Senate bills without notice to other lawmakers, among other indignities.

Hastert was able to pull all this off largely because, after the scandal-plagued speakerships of Gingrich and Livingston, he presented as a normie heartland Republican, rumpled and affable, to cite the preferred term in most of the pre-scandal media coverage of his speakership. But his brand of corruptionism was no less damaging or toxic than DeLay’s—and in touting his eponymous rule, he fatally set the House GOP conference on the hypervigilant ideological course that’s seen it cannibalize many of his successor speakers in fits of performative purity. And the broad logic of the Hastert rule has fanned out into the party’s electoral strategizing—creating an ever-expanding contingent of bright red gerrymandered districts, custom-made to produce the kind of feckless ideologues that routinely deadlock plans to fund the government—and thereby set up follow-on speaker purges. Given the state of today’s Republican Party, Michael Johnson should strike a blow for historical accuracy and restore Hastert’s portrait to the Capitol.
